POSSIBLE THREAT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA COAST-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave of the House under Standing Order 43 to present a motion of urgent and pressing necessity arising out of the pending conclusion to a hearing which may reach a decision on the establishment of an oil tanker route on the Pacific coast of Canada. In light of the recent suggestions by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) that Canadians should speak out, and in light of the fact that Canadians in British Columbia are speaking out in the form of a petition, I ask leave of the House to move the following motion, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard):
The House of Commons express its appreciation that the Legislative Assembly of the province of British Columbia unanimously passed the undermentioned resolution namely:
"That this House expresses to the federal government their deep misgivings over the ecological disaster which will engulf the coast of British Columbia following the construction of a trans-Alaska pipeline and attendant super tanker transport of oil off the coast of British Columbia.
We ask the federal government to use every available resource at their disposal to persuade the American government to use alternate methods of transporting crude oil from Alaska to the United States."
And further this House of Commons urges the government to carry out the wishes of the legislature of the province of British Columbia forthwith.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Some days ago the leader of the House on the government side drew attention to the difficulty which arises in our proceedings under Standing Order 43 in that an explanation by the member who seeks to move such a motion is permitted but no opportunity is provided for anyone who may object to the motion to indicate his reason for doing so. subtopic: POSSIBLE THREAT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA COAST-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext: Order. The hon. member knows the terms of the Standing Order. They are very simple. The Chair has to determine whether there is unanimity. As I pointed out the other day, and I think I should reiterate it, it is not the consent of the government which is sought in accordance with the Standing Order but the consent of the House. Any one member, even from the party of the hon. member who is proposing the motion, can object and the motion cannot be put. When there is not unanimity, the moment an hon. member on one side or another of the House calls "no" or indicates he is not prepared to give his consent, the motion cannot be put. It is as simple as that. I would not think it would be in order to invite anyone to indicate, on his own behalf, why he is withholding consent.

The House resumed from Friday, February 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benson that Bill C-219, to establish the Canada Development Corporation, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs and the amendment thereto of Mr. Saltsman (page 3648).

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a three-word phrase, "Canada Development Corporation" is a success. There is a certain ring to it that is pleasant to the ear as well as to the mind. We are all in favour of the development of Canada, and we want that development, to the fullest possible extent, to be done by and for Canadians. This is not because we are chauvinistic, but because we believe it is normal that any country make its own internal decisions in its own interests. Any country wants its own citizens to have the necessary skills to play a predominant part in its own development, and any country wants to ensure that its own priorities are respected. We believe too that, even in an economy such as ours, where decision-making is largely a private and decentralized matter, there is certainly an important place for the central government to encourage economic development.
In the past year, we have witnessed the power of the central government to harm the economy through the deliberate creation of mass unemployment. I have said time and time again that the decisions which led to the present situation were bad decisions, and I shall continue to say so. They were decisions that displayed the essential character of this government, arrogance and unconcern. But they also illustrated the power that lies with the federal government. They illustrated the importance of the decisions that are made right here in Ottawa; and they demonstrate the necessity for careful use of that power today and in the future. It is not the government that is going to develop Canada. It is the people of this country who are going to do that. But the federal government has a tremendous amount of power that it can use either to encourage that development or to hamper it. This power must be used with foresight and imagination. And it must be applied with care.
The general idea of a Canada Development Corporation is a defensible one. But we are not faced here today with a general idea. We are faced with a specific piece of
[Mr. Gray.)
March 2, 1971

legislation which we must judge as best we can. And as soon as we begin to look at this bill, difficulties begin to appear. They begin to appear, in fact, when we look at the self-proclaimed goals of this legislation.
First, we are told that the CDC is supposed to help develop and maintain Canadian presence in private industry in this country. Then, we are informed that the corporation is designed to give greater opportunities to Canadians to invest profitably in Canadian industry. In themselves, these two goals are not necessarily incompatible; but neither are they one and the same thing. There will inevitably be occasions when they do come into conflict with one another. This raises the question as to the situation of the directors who are to have the responsibility for running the corporation. In the normal course of events, the goal of a company director must be to work in the interests of the shareholders of the corporation, which is to say that his goal must be the maximization of profits. However, this corporation will be different in that it is a government-sponsored corporation and therefore, presumably, is to some extent at least responsible to the people of Canada. From that aspect, the directors must always consider the national interest. They must remember that one of the aims of the corporation is to help develop the Canadian sector of the economy.
One has only to raise the question to see that right at the very base of the Canada Development Corporation, as envisaged in the present bill, there is ambiguity and confusion. The question that poses itself immediately is the following: Will the CDC, in the form it is given under this bill, be anything more than a publicly sponsored private investment company working along the traditional lines for the interest of the people who hold shares in it? Is this what it is? Is it anything more than a publicly sponsored private investment company? If it is something more, what more precisely is it supposed to be? After all, a vague statement of goals is simply not enough. In other words, apart from the question of the maximization of profit, what else are the directors of this corporation suppose to achieve? It is all very well to say that they should work in the national interest as well as the interest of the shareholders, but what does this mean in practice? To what extent if any will the national interest justify or indeed require investments offering less than maximum profits to the shareholders of the corporation? Let us take a specific example.
We are told that the CDC, if it so desires, will be able to take over Polymer Corporation. This firm is currently making money for the government and, therefore, for the Canadian taxpayer. How will the directors of the CDC view the national interest when they are negotiating the price to pay for Polymer Corporation? In the interest of its own shareholders, CDC must, of course, pay the lowest possible price, but in the interests of the Canadian people it should pay the highest possible price for Polymer. There is an interesting conundrum, and one that points out once again the ambiguity that lies at the base of this measure.
Let us look at the more general picture. Supposing the CDC, as it is proposed, had an opportunity to participate
23966-33i
Canada Development Corporation
in a development which was widely considered as one that ought to be controlled by Canadians. Supposing this was the general impression in the country. Suppose there was reason to believe that such a development could stay afloat, but it would be likely to produce only very low profits for the Canadian owners. In other words; this would be a case where you would have low profitability versus considerations of national interest as widely understood in the country. Where does the responsibility of the directors of this corporation lie? To what extent, if any, should they take lower profits to achieve Canadian participation in such a development even though it means substantially lower profits to the shareholders of the CDC? That is not an easy question to answer. It is certainly not easy to answer from reading this legislation. It will be all the more difficult, because in such a case the corporation would inevitably be subject to tremendous pressures from opposite directions, economic from the shareholders on the one hand and political, social and nationalistic from the government and organized public opinion on the other.
I feel sincerely sorry for the eventual directors of such a corporation. I hope that none of them will have any latent tendencies toward a split personality, because they wouldn't be helped any by having to work within the schizophrenic structures and goals that this present measure is setting out.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Given this schizophrenia in the bill, it is not surprising that criticism of it has also gone in different directions. Some critics on the left charge that the CDC as proposed would be nothing more nor less than a giant government-sponsored investment corporation designed to provide another profitable outlet for the money of corporations and of wealthy Canadians. On the other hand, there are those who say that this is simply another step toward socialism. In the words of the Globe and Mail, and I quote:
The CDC will be, in the public mind, a Crown Corporation, subject in Parliament to all the political pressures of the electorate's nationalism and caution, inhibited from the boldness and ruthlessness that is essential to success.
With its usual complacency, this government through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) says that, being criticized on both sides like that, it must be right. Things are not that simple. Things are not that simple because, in this case, both criticisms-contradictory though they might be-are at least partially valid. Each one puts the spotlight on a major weakness of the present bill. The first points up the fact that there is nothing in the proposed CDC to define exactly what the directors may properly consider other than maximum profits of the shareholders of the CDC. The second points to the fact that neither is there any assurance that the proposed body would act with any consistency in the interests of its shareholders. The question must therefore be asked: What is the relevance of this bill to the whole question of Canadian control over our own economy? And what is its

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation relevance for that matter to the whole question of economic development in the national interest? The provisional answer must be that there is no evidence that it is relevant in either case.
The point is that there are many, many questions left unanswered both by the present bill and by the whole concept of the CDC that is contained in the present bill. For example, there are questions that have been raised by economists as to whether, even were they possible, the tasks, as laid down in the present government proposals, are realistically desirable.
This measure is based on the assumption that it is the shortage of capital which is the main reason not only for foreign take-over of Canadian firms, but also for the general lack of development ventures that are taking place under Canadian control. However, as several economists have pointed out, there may well be several reasons other than the unavailability of Canadian capital to explain the situation. There are a variety of reasons why foreign interests may be able to offer far more for control of a Canadian company than Canadian interests can offer. Similarly, there are a variety of reasons why a particular Canadian development might be far more profitable for a foreign owner than for a Canadian owner. It might be, for example, that the technological resources at the disposal of a large United States corporation would be the deciding factor in some cases. It might be, too, that the resources of a foreign corporation, as well as its requirements, would play a deciding role in many instances, making it worth while for a foreign corporation to pay considerably more, meaning that control of, or participation in, a Canadian development was much more profitable for a foreign corporation.
Then, of course there is the whole question of the comparative tax structure as between Canada and other countries. We have had occasion to raise some questions about this. Economists such as Professor Neufeld have pointed out that the availability of capital is not the only consideration. In that event, the CDC as envisaged in this bill could involve an approach which would be altogether inappropriate to our needs, especially when one considers the schizophrenic nature of the corporation to which I have already referred.
Presumably, we will be given answers to some of the questions I have raised presumably we shall be given some of the reasons why there is so much foreign takeover, why outside interests are in so many cases controlling our resources. Presumably some of these answers will be contained in the report on the whole subject of foreign investment which is supposed to be tabled in the near future-the "Gray" paper, if I may refer to it as such. Certainly, we ought to get a good many answers. Before being asked to establish the CDC we ought to have before us the government's analysis of the reasons we are losing control of the economy and the reason Canadians are not participating more fully in the development of that economy. We ought to be told the measures the

government proposes to take in the light of this analysis of the situation.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext: Why, for example, are we faced with a bill which talks pretentiously about the public interest without ever defining that public interest, and making no effort to show how it is to be achieved? Why are we faced with a bill which involves a modification of the tax structure in the realm of investment at precisely the time when the Canadian people are living in a climate of extreme uncertainty as to the government's intentions with regard to tax reform? We are still waiting to find out what the government intends to do about investment incentive in general. Why this piecemeal approach, now? Why are we faced now with a bill which touches on the field of foreign investment when in a few weeks, we are told, we are to receive the long awaited report of the government on foreign investment in Canada? This brings me to the general question: why has this bill been brought in now? What affected its timing? After hanging around for eight years, the concept of the CDC has suddenly been dusted off and presented as an example of the determination of the government to protect Canadian industry and help Canadians develop Canada. The question many people are asking is: why could the government not have waited until the appearance of its report on foreign control of our industry? The Minister of Finance, in his genial way, disarmingly replied that the bill was being presented now simply because it is ready.

speechtext:
They are finding the going a little heavy. I suggest another reason is this. Had the government
March 2, 1971

waited for the report on foreign ownership, the "Gray" paper, it would have been forced to take a comprehensive look at this whole question. It might have been obliged to take a stand on the issue of economic nationalism and its relationship to Canada's economic development and economic identity. By coming out with this flashy but irrelevant proposition, the government hopes to take the pressures off before the report comes forward in the form of the "Gray" paper.
I can tell the government that whatever happens to this empty measure before us, the pressures will not be off. The Canadian people and this Parliament want to know where the government stands, if indeed it stands anywhere. This bill is authentic in one way. It is another reflection of the uncertainty and ambiguity which characterized the government in its economic and social policies. This bill, and the so-called CDC it is supposed to spawn, takes all the emptiness, the uncertainties and the ambiguities of the government's policies and rolls them into one meaningless package.
To expose its hollowness, one has only to ask: what would have happened had the CDC been in operation at the time of the sale of Ryerson Press? From the standpoint of national interest and national concern there would have been tremendous pressure, both moral and political, for the CDC to step in and save one of the few remaining Canadian textbook publishers. But from the standpoint of profit, evidently there would have been no way in which the CDC could properly have become involved. This appears to be obvious. Either way, the response of the directors of the CDC would have been bitterly disputed.
Let us not forget there will be many occasions in the future when there will be clear conflict between national interest, or what appears to be the national interest in the eyes of many Canadians, and the profitability of a particular deal. This is why it is inevitable that any sort of publicly-sponsored development corporation of this kind would be embroiled up to the hilt in political pressures of all kinds. If it succumbs to these pressures, the shareholders will suffer, and if it does not, there will be a tremendous amount of disillusionment on the part of those who really see this organization as an instrument for preserving Canada as they see Canada. In short, Mr. Speaker, I think this measure in its present form, offered at the present time, is both futile and dangerous. It is futile because there is no evidence that it will be relevant to the national interest it is supposed to defend, and its merit is certainly unpredictable to the eventual shareholders it is supposed to benefit.
Leaving aside for the moment the question of Canadian control, let us look simply at the question of risk. If this corporation is really to serve Canadian development in a way that private investors cannot, it is going to have to take risks. It is going to have to invest money in spheres where not only is there no sure return, but there is no return available in the near future, and where such
Canada Development Corporation return as there may be is remote in time and relatively low in amount. That is why I really wonder just how the government plans to appeal to the potential shareholders of the CDC. Will it be an appeal in the name of patriotism, or will it be an appeal in the name of self-interest? The government has at least given itself lots of time before issuing that appeal. In fact, I have already predicted that the appeal will never come, regardless whether or not this bill is passed, and I make the same prediction today. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the government will never issue shares in the CDC, at least not in this CDC, because the whole concept is too confused, too ambiguous and too self-contradictory.
I have said that this measure is futile. It is also a dangerous piece of legislation, dangerous because of the disillusionment that would result from its failure in the sphere of national interest and development, which would be proportionate to the hopes that it would raise. I do not want to see disillusionment and cynicism among our people about the future of our country; but by falsely raising hopes, this sort of bill would certainly contribute to that result.
Full of contradictions and confusions in its goals as in its methods, what is the purpose of such a bill? The minister himself admits that it is useless to small business, as it is to regional development. Certainly it will be of no use at all to small business in this country. The one million dollar minimum investment called for in the bill is a guarantee that no help will be available to small businessmen, as we understand that expression. Certainly, it will be of no use in the fight against regional disparity. On the contrary, the criterion of maximum profitability will, if anything, act as an effective damper on any suggestion that we take a chance on a poorer region.

With the usual vague words and pretentious language, the government is out to convince the Canadian people that it really cares-in fact, that it cares doubly. It cares about Canadian control over the economy, and it cares about economic development. So do we all, Mr. Speaker. But in this case, it is only the government that can act. This is why we of the opposition are so keenly disappointed that this government has once

Canada Development Corporation again preferred image to substance and come up with a hybrid and unworkable monstrosity that is of no use to anybody except the ever-busy image builders in the employ of the government.
In reality this is a shoddy public relations gimmick which is designed to refurbish the image of this government among those millions of Canadians who do care very deeply about what happens to this country. This whole area is too important to the Canadian people to reject out of hand any and all action that must be taken. However, I do feel that we cannot accept this hasty and ill-conceived bill as it now stands.
I, therefore, give notice that a member of the official opposition will be moving a reasoned amendment to refer the subject matter of this bill to committee to be considered when we receive the Gray report as to the real situation regarding foreign ownership, and when we receive the package of measures that the government proposes to take as well as the government's legislative proposals regarding tax reform and changes in the tax structure.
We think that the sensible course to take with regard to a measure such as this is to refer it to a committee to try to make some sense out of it in light of the general program that the government will be putting forward. But if this proposal is refused and the government does not refer the bill to committee with this sort of directive, we shall have no alternative but to vote against this particular measure on second reading. If this government has any sense of responsibility toward the Canadian people it will accept our suggestion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deeply regret that the legislation before the House, Bill C-219 to establish the Canada Development Corporation, is throwing away a golden opportunity to contribute to the solution of one of Canada's basic problems. I refer to the problem of regional disparities.

At the 1969 constitutional conference the governments in Canada declared as follows:
This constitutional conference agrees that the promotion of the full development of all parts of Canada is an essential objective of confederation.
On February 8 and 9 of this year, the third working session of the constitutional conference recalled the conclusion reached on the subject of regional disparities by the working session of the previous September. The first ministers agreed that the constitution should include a recognition of the importance of equality of opportunity for all Canadians.
This, it said, should not only be in the new preamble to the constitution but in the body of the constitution. The preamble should state that one objective of Confederation is the social, economic, and cultural opportunity for all citizens in whatever region they may live. The Constitutional Conference went on to say that in the body of the constitution there should be a statement of obligation on all governments, federal and provincial, to promote equality of opportunity and well being of all individuals, to ensure, as nearly as possible, that essential public services of reasonable quality will be available to individual citizens, and to promote economic development which will reduce disparities in the social and economic opportunities of individual Canadians in whatever region they may live. These pronouncements would enshrine in our fundamental law the obligation to deal with regional inequalities.
Nevertheless, the present legislation throws away an essential tool in implementing these basic national purposes. It fails to maintain public control by giving into the interests of individual shareholders. It stresses maximization of profit. It gives no more than impotent minority rights to those representing the public interest and it makes sure that what should be a basic purpose of the Canada Development Corporation is ignored.
A major cause of disparities in the social and economic opportunities for Canadians in the different regions has been the natural tendency of those who control private investment to channel their investments into central Canada in search of maximum profitability. It is precisely this that a properly constituted and equipped CDC would remedy. The Canada Development Corporation proposed by this legislation entirely fails for this purpose.
The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) has pointed out in this debate and on many other occasions that the conception of a Canada Development Corporation held by this party is that it is something that can and will act as an instrument of Canadian government policy and secure Canadian objectives. He has said:
In our view, the CDC should be involved in regional development policies with provincial bodies and agencies in order to ensure that every part of Canada capable of supporting viable development is extensively involved in the industrial future of this country.
It seems to me that the future unity of this country depends upon the federal government demonstrating that
March 2, 1971

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation buying back foreign controlled industries, except perhaps in certain limited cases where an opportunity presents itself.
I believe the resources of the Canada Development Corporation should be available, subject to proper research and adequate planning, for investment in the development of Canada as a whole. That is what is lacking in the present legislation. In 1968 the Economic Council of Canada pointed out that:
Nowhere in the federal government structure is there a central focus-to ensure the allocation of funds to secure the maximum benefits for the region and the country as a whole. There is a clear need for a complete reappraisal of administration and procedural means of putting federal support of the Atlantic Regional Development on a more rational and well-integrated basis.
Has this changed with the creation of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and its new programs? The answer is no. As recently as last Wednesday in the House of Commons, as recorded at page 3709 of Hansard, the minister in reply to a question by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) said that his department could not co-ordinate its activities under the Regional Development Incentives Act with the responsibilities of other departments. Thus, the hoped for coordination and central focus in government has not been achieved.
In the report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on Canada-U.S. relations, the evidence of Mr. Claude Lemelin is quoted as follows:
We might even ask if the new federal incentive programs for investment in the underdeveloped areas will be able to modify by themselves, the repartition of investments and employment in favour of these areas. And this is because the private investments, which result more often than not from decisions taken in the U.S., are not in agreement with the Canadian development requirements which are based on east-west axis, but are in terms of continental requirements, i.e. a north-south axis-
A publicly directed Canada development corporation such as has been proposed by this party in the nature of a Crown corporation, borrowing its funds from the Canadian public by bonds and by required investment of some part of the funds available from financial institutions in Canada, could do this essential job for Canada. The Canada Development Corporation created by this legislation will be torn between profit maximization and concern for national interests. It will be directed by those with a traditional outlook. It will not be subject to direction of the government or the interests of national policies. Its only justification is that it is a sop to economic nationalism.
It might be asked why a representative of Ontario and Toronto-by no means a disadvantaged area when it comes to regional disparity-should be raising an issue which is of more direct importance to other regions such as the Maritime provinces, perhaps Quebec, and some of the western provinces. I raise this question because I believe in the long-run it is in the enlightened self-interest of all parts of Canada, including central Canada and Ontario, that regional disparity be ironed out and that depressed areas be given special attention in the invest-

ment policies of Canada. Canadian unity requires this and in the long-run the prosperity and well-being of Canada require it. It is just too bad that a wonderful opportunity to establish an effective instrument to this end is being allowed to go down the drain.
Instead of legislation to provide for effective mobilization of Canadian resources for Canadian purposes, we are asked to accept a phony substitute. We are getting a fagade in place of the real thing. The House should reject this bill or should accept the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is now considering a very significant piece of legislation, that is Bill C-219. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has voiced his objection to the overall bill. Personally, I have looked pretty closely at this bill and I think hon. members are entitled to question the advisability of introducing at this stage of the session a bill which at first sight appears to be most important.
As far as the principle of this act is concerned, I hardly believe that any member would object to it on the basis of the contents of clause 2 which reads as follows:
The purpose of this Act is to establish a corporation that will help develop and maintain strong Canadian controlled and managed corporations in the private sector of the economy and will give Canadians greater opportunities to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada.
If we confine ourselves to clause 2 of the bill, it seems to me that all hon. members should support it. This bill purports to encourage Canadians to invest in Canadian companies instead of investing, as they did in former times, in foreign companies established in Canada which reinvest their funds outside our country. Indeed we have often seen Canadians lend money to foreign finance or insurance companies which reinvested it in foreign countries and not in Canada, and in this way channelled the savings of the Canadian people into foreign companies.
If one of the aims of this semi-public corporation is to encourage Canadian people to invest in Canadian firms so that the latter become full partners in the industrial development of this country, I will say that this is a very commendable intent indeed.
But how could we believe it without having a deeper knowledge of the direction the government is going to take with its so-called economic nationalism policy?
Briefly, this is the policy of this government respecting the operations of foreign companies in Canada. We recall that during the last electoral campaign the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) as well as the members of his cabinet and of his party, realized certain electoral benefits from this economic nationalism.
For the last three years, Mr. Speaker, this government was to provide clear-cut leadership to Canadians and policy statements made on the subject either by the Miniter of Finance (Mr. Benson) or members of the cabinet have so far been obscure, hesitant and timid.
March 2, 1971

One cannot talk about a Canadian Development Corporation without a thorough knowledge of this government's policy on foreign concerns operating in Canada. Will the CDC be strong enough, both from the management and capital standpoint, to compete equitably and viably with foreign corporations?
When the bill was introduced, the hon. Minister of Finance did not speak on that aspect. We are justified in asking the government today to take a firm, unequivocal attitude, so that Canadians who invest in this new corporation will be able to assess in advance the risk of their investment.
If I understood the objects of this corporation correctly, it should first seek to invest its equity in the establishment of new industries and in the expansion of industries which have already proved profitable and viable; in short, this corporation should be an effective incentive for the creation of new jobs. If this is a priority-and it should be a priority for the government, in view of the disastrous unemployment situation in which Canada now finds itself, when 8 per cent of the work force is idle and when Quebec has 243,000 unemployed'-I say this should be a long term program to create jobs.
As stated this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition, we know that this Corporation will not immediately assist small concerns. It will again be meant to help large industries. Today, as I just said, when economic conditions in Canada are disastrous as far as employment is concerned, the government must take various means in order to help small industries.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is already trying to attain that objective. We know that the department was indeed trying to create new industries to promote the development of small concerns and boost employment in Canada. Perhaps the Quebec members have read in weekend newspapers that the problem exists everywhere in Quebec, especially where the doldrums are so acute that they are discouraging for some classes of society.
During the weekend Mr. Speaker-and I think that this is related to the subject of this debate-I attended a meeting in Sacre-Coeur in the Saguenay constituency. Those people have been working for 8 years at the development of a cardboard manufacture with the co-operation of the CFU. By the way, the CFU spent $200,000 solely for the industrial promotion of that plant.
Mr. Speaker, people get discouraged when they see that the government does not intervene, when circumstances warrant it, to assist more directly in establishing industries that would create employment.
At Sacre-Cceur, Mr. Speaker, we have seeked to get Quebecers and Americans interested in setting up a cardboard factory. The Catholic Farmers Union did what it could, spending $200,000 for that purpose. Now, the experts' report assures us of the viability of that factory, but $25 million would be needed to implement the project.
Canada Development Corporation
Could the Minister of Finance indicate whether, once Bill C-219 to establish the Canada Development Corporation is enacted, it will overlap the purposes and objectives of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion?
To come back to the example I mentioned a moment ago with regard to Sacre-Cceur, in Saguenay County, if the regulations of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion are followed, a grant of $6.5 million will be paid to this plant in order to create 500 jobs, that is $30,000 per job. I would like the minister to tell us whether this act could not be invoked to finance the balance of $17 million required to establish the cardboard factory at Sacre-Coeur.
I think that the minister should be able to answer our questions.
Once again, I want to know whether the Canadian Development Corporation will duplicate the Department of Regional Economic Expansion or whether it will merely make it disappear. To my mind, the people are worried.
One must admit that department has helped the people in some respects. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) recently stated that since his department was set up, 60,000 jobs have been created; still, the minister must tell us whether this new act is intended to complement the services of his department or merely to replace them.
Will the CDC also be authorized, as I said a while ago, to have access to the funds of the Canadian government when there will be a financial contribution from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion?
Mr. Speaker, the new corporation must be structured in such a way as to avoid the errors of the General Investment Corporation of Quebec.
First of all, we must know if the corporation will compete with organized financing companies operating in several provinces of Canada. Is there provision for investment planning in this corporation in co-operation with other companies of a semi-public or private nature operating in other provinces of Canada? Will this new corporation extend preferential rates to its shareholders so that finance corporations in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada will find themselves in a precarious situation?
We must avoid the mistakes that have been made by the Quebec General Investment Corporation whose objectives are similar to those spelt out in Bill C-219. We believe that the discomfiture of the Quebec General Investment Corporation in some areas can be attributed to the human factor. It may be that the men who set up this financial system lacked the necessary competence.
In many case, the Quebec General Investment Corporation has not been able so far to appeal to serious investors who could have turned it into a stable institution from an economic and financial point of view. This Corporation stopped paying quarterly dividends in September last.

Since its inception eight years ago, the Quebec General Investment Corporation has not been able to gain the confidence of investors because the value of its share on the Montreal Stock Exchange has never gone over the $10 mark of their face value. They are presently trading at $8.50 after considerable variations over the last eight years. If the new legislation introduced by the Minister of Finance seeks to achieve the same objectives as those aimed at by the Quebec General Investment Corporation, I believe that the minister and the cabinet must closely consider the mechanism and structures of the said Corporation: as everybody knows, it is now going through difficult times.
Although its aggregate firms are well established, the General Investment Corporation has met with unequal results. In fact, not so long ago, SOGEFOR folded. On the other hand, the SOMA almost went down many times; it was also financed by the General Investment Corporation. In 1969, before amortization, it had lost $346,000. The largest subsidiary, Marine Industries, registered a 48 per cent loss on its net profits for 1969, and its shareholders are now impatiently awaiting its financial report for the current fiscal year.
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday last, Entreprises Soucy, a Riviere-du-Loup pulp and paper industry in which the General Investment Corporation had invested funds, closed its doors. It laid off 200 people. To reopen, the firm needs over $1 million.
The Montreal newspaper La presse, under the signature of Mr. Jacques Tremblay, has published an article in which the life of the General Investment Corporation was described as follows:
When the General Investment Corporation was created in 1963, people still entertained very optimistic ideas: "everything is possible", "we shall achieve a quiet revolution". A series of well-defined operations were to make us masters in our own home: nationalization of electricity, deposit fund, investment corporation, replacement of family enterprises by modern "industrial complexes", and so forth.
-Every project based upon an old national economic mythology seemed like another step towards paradise. In the end, there are naturally a few downfalls. Our professorial economics proved more effective at making speeches than at controlling our economy.
The seventies should be the decade of realism. Should the minor downfalls of the General Investment Corporation help us to become conscious of that fact, they will have proved useful. Of course, the fanfare accompanying every move of the General Investment Corporation is now likely to create some kind of defeatism in the face of its difficulties. But such defeatism is no more founded than the fanfare.
Mr. Speaker, this shows that the aims of the General Investment Corporation are apparently similar to those of the measure now before us. It should be a lesson to us before we lay the foundations of the Canada Development Corporation.

If moreover, this corporation enters into competition with existing provincial investment corporations their economic influence and power will surely be jeopardized. It is therefore logical, Mr. Speaker, to draw the following conclusions:
First, the government must make sure that the Canada Development Corporation will consult the provinces as to the operation of similar corporations having similar objectives.
Secondly, since the CDC will be wholly financed first through public funds and later on through public outlays, it is essential for Parliament to supervise and control its operation.
Thirdly, why would the law not give Parliament the right to ask this semi-public and semi-private corporation, that will use taxpayers' money, to report on its operation to the people's elected representatives?
Fourthly, how can we avoid that CDC's competition be detrimental to our existing financial institutions such as banks, trust companies, mutual funds and other similar organizations which, thanks to their structure and their operations, have already rendered valuable services to Canadians?
As the hon. Leader of the Opposition said a moment ago, some clauses of the bill are so vague that the government must absolutely accept his proposal so as to enable us to know the CDC's financial structure before ereating this organization so important to the Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the minister is a responsible man since he is in charge of the taxpayers' money. Doubtless he will accept the proposal which was made by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon and which would enable us to study this bill more thoroughly and to know all its consequences.
But if the minister is so impatient to have it adopted, it is because he is looking forward to the presidency of this new corporation. He hopes to secure a new position for the future as has already been done by the former Minister of Transport who is now the President of the Canadian Transport Commission. If it is so urgent for the minister to get this position, I am prepared to vote right away in favour of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill to set up a Canada Development Corporation could have been a legislative landmark heralding a new era for economic development in Canada and the maintenance of a much greater degree of Canadian economic independence. Unfortunately, the government has approached the matter both reluctantly and half-heartedly. The minister's speech the other day gave one the impression that he was introducing this measure merely to fulfil some of the political commitments that had been made by his predecessors. Let me just review briefly the history of the idea of a Canada Development Corporation.
March 2, 1971

The New Democratic Party at its founding convention in 1961 put forward the idea of a publicly owned and publicly controlled Canada Development Corporation as a means of expanding the Canadian economy and of guaranteeing a greater measure of Canadian economic independence. In the election of 1962, we fought the campaign with that as one of the major issues. In 1963, Hon. Walter Gordon, who at that time was masterminding the Liberal campaign, put the concept of a Canada Development Corporation at the masthead of the Liberal campaign. When the government came to office after the election of 1963, Mr. Gordon, who at that time was minister of finance, introduced a measure on June 20, 1965, for the setting up of a Canada Development Corporation. Of course, it caused great distress in the ranks of the corporate establishment. Apparently, tremendous pressure was brought to bear on the newly elected Liberal government and the measure was dropped.
Then, in March, 1966, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), who then was Minister of Finance, said that the Canada development proposal would be introduced, "as soon as the parliamentary timetable permits." In October, 1966, Prime Minister Pearson denied that this project had been shelved. In July, 1967, the minister of finance of the day, who now is Secretary of State for External Affairs, said that a draft of the Canada Development Corporation bill would be ready for cabinet shortly. In March, 1968, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) called the Canada Development Corporation a "valuable tool". It was promised to the people of Canada in the Speech from the Throne in September, 1968. In that month of that year the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said, "I have the CDC bill in my hand. I expect to introduce it as soon as my fall budget is through." In April, 1969, the Minister of Finance said that he hoped to present a draft of the CDC proposal to the cabinet in the summer.
This has been long awaited legislation, Mr. Speaker, and now it is here. It is a pale version of what was first proposed by Mr. Gordon in 1965.

speechtext:
It certainly is a completely emasculated version of what the New Democratic Party has been talking about since 1961. It is quite apparent that the opposition of the corporate elite in this country has forced the Minister of Finance to denigrate and emasculate this concept so that we have before us today a legislative monstrosity. Someone said that a camel is the picture of a horse drawn by a committee bent on compromise. Certainly, that is exactly the kind of distortion that has finally emerged from seven years of Liberal gestation. I said, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is a monstrosity. I say so for three distinct reasons.
First, Mr. Speaker, under this legislation the taxpayers of Canada will take all the financial risks, and a comparatively small group of investors will get the major part of any profits which may eventually accrue to this enterprise. Under this measure the government will em-
Canada Development Corporation bark on what the minister calls a partnership. Speaking on February 22, as reported at page 3640 of Hansard, the minister said this about the Canada Development Corporation:
It will represent a new and significant partnership between the public and private sectors in the dynamic development of our economy.
Let us look at the Liberal party's idea of a partnership. This is a partnership in which the people of this country will put up, under this legislation, initially some $350 million, $250 million in equity capital and a loan of $100 million. In addition, the government will turn over to the corporation the assets of certain Crown corporations, valued anywhere from $300 million to $400 million. This money and these assets are being put up by all the taxpayers of this country, by the poor, the disadvantaged, the ordinary workers, the farmers and old age pensioners who pay taxes into the federal treasury. Yet, if this corporation does not operate successfully, they will lose the money which this government has invested.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. He implied that the money invested would be tax revenue raised by the government of Canada. I am sure that he did not mean to leave that implication in his statement. It will, instead, be money raised by the government of Canada through the issuance of bonds.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Of
course. Yet surely the minister is not naive enough to think, and surely he does not think the public is naive enough to think, that if the government puts $350 million in cash plus all the assets of some Crown corporations into Canada Development Corporation, and the corporation fails, that the Canadian taxpayer will not have to make good the loss. In the event of failure, the responsibility being assumed by the government of Canada will be met by the taxpayers of this country. It is the money of the taxpayers which is being used. If there are losses, the Canadian people as a whole will have to pay. If the corporation is a success, as I hope, then it is clear that the major part of the profits will go to that small sector of the Canadian economy which is able to invest, probably between 7 per cent and 10 per cent of the population of Canada.
When I was a boy we used to play a game called "put-and-take". You put so much into the pot, and if you got a lucky number you were able to take. This bill, too, is like a put-and-take game.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext: It is a gamble.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The
Canadian people will put in the money and take all the risks; and if the corporation is successful the investment groups in the country will take the major part of the profits. This is the liberal idea of a partnership. The government takes comfort from the fact that it will be the largest shareholder and that its share will not go below 10 per cent. It may well be the largest shareholder, but it may not necessarily be the controlling shareholder.

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
A combination of companies each holding, say, 3 per cent of the equity of this corporation could well form the controlling group. Of the 18 or 21 directors on the board, only four, unless the government chooses the other option, will represent the government. The other alternative would be for the board to vote according to the number of voting shares held; but the government has given no assurance whatever that it intends to seek that alternative.
It is significant that the bill itself provides that the corporation is not responsible to Parliament. The people of Canada are being asked to underwrite a corporation that is not responsible to Parliament, not responsible to the elected representatives of the people. What we are going to have is a partnership in which the Canadian people take all the chances, undergo all the risks, put up in the initial stages all the money and assets and, if this project succeeds, then eventually those who are able to buy stock in this company will own 90 per cent and the Canadian taxpayers will own 10 per cent.
The second reason why I call this bill a monstrosity is that it proposes to sell out four Crown corporations. It proposes to sell the Polymer Corporation, which produces synthetic rubber and which has been a very successful operation; the Eldorado Mining Company; the Northern Transportation and the government's 45 per cent equity in Panarctic Oil. Later, if the government decides by order in council, it will sell Northern Transportation.
The minister has never explained why the Canadian people are being asked to go from 100 per cent ownership of these public enterprises to an eventual 10 per cent ownership. The Canadian people took all the risks. The Canadian people pioneered these projects. They have been brought to a point where they are self sustaining, and in some cases, revenue producing. Why does the government now propose to turn them over to a corporation of which the Canadian people will eventually own only a 10 per cent equity? As his reason for this, the minister stated on February 22, as recorded at page 3640 of Hansard:
Some of these enterprises are in a position where their further growth and development could be facilitated by giving them the greater flexibility to operate and better access to capital markets which would come from CDC ownership of their shares.
Do they lack flexibility now, Mr. Speaker? Polymer Corporation has branched out into a wide variety of activities, even outside this country. Do they lack access to capital? No one in this country can borrow money as cheaply and easily as the government of Canada. The government is really saying that it wants to divest itself of these public enterprises now that they have become successful.
If the government were really interested in developing the public sector of economy, the government could provide both the flexibility and access to the capital requirement to expand these industries rather than turning over 90 per cent of them to the private sector. This means that

the ordinary people of this country whose tax money or credit has been used to develop these Crown corporations are now going to see their share reduced from 100 per cent to 10 per cent. I think that this is a sop which the Liberal government is offering to their friends in the corporate structure at the expense of the Canadian people. This is exactly what the Liberal government did after World War II, when they took Crown corporations which had been set up during the war to provide essential economic services and sold them at firesale prices to the corporate establishment of this country. This action by the present government betrays the Liberal party's bias toward the financial establishment and its basic dislike of public ownership. After this demonstration, let's have no more talk by the Liberal party about its belief in public ownership.
The third reason why I have described this Canada Development Corporation, as envisaged by this government, as a monstrosity is that it will not be an instrument of national policy. The sole value of setting up a Canada Development Corporation is that it should be enabled to do the things which the private sector of the economy has either been unable or unwilling to do. Some years ago when I was involved in the matter of the industrial development agency in the province of Saskatchewan, I visited a number of countries to study the question of government development corporations. Whether you go to the Scandinavian countries, West Germany, Italy, France or Israel, you will find that in each of these instances the government's industrial agency is used as an instrument of national policy to do things for the nation as a whole. This government is proposing to turn that responsibility over to a private corporation in which the maximization of profit will be the principle motivation.
In Israel, where most of the large industrial enterprises are on a tripartite basis, one third of the equity is held by the government of Israel through its industrial development corporation, one third held by the Histdruth, which is the co-operative trade union organization and one third is held by private companies, many of them foreign, which also have the management contract to operate the business. This gives to those areas the best of both worlds. They get the benefit of the technical knowhow, expertise, managerial skill and the patents of private entrepreneurs while at the same time keeping the control of the industry in the hands of the people of that country and retaining two thirds of the profits in the country where it is being earned.
The minister made a passing reference to which I want to refer. I quote from page 3639 of Hansard:
We do not want another fiasco such as the one in Saskatchewan when the present leader of the NDP was Premier of that province.
I am not going to spend the time of the House discussing Saskatchewan. I do not mind if some Liberal backbencher out of a vast sea of ignorance makes comments about Saskatchewan, but the Minister of Finance (Mr. March 2, 1971

Benson) has access to the records and knows much better. He has on his staff some of the people who were largely responsible for carrying out the programs and policies of that government. He knows the facts. He knows that in the 20 years in which there was a CCF government in Saskatchewan, all the public sector, that part which was monopolistic, public utilities such as telephones, the sale and distribution of electric power and natural gas, showed a return of 9 per cent. The balance of the public sector, which covered such things as insurance, sodium sulphate, bus transportation and Northern Air Lines, showed a return of 16 per cent. That is not a bad record. Reference was made to the fact that a shoe factory or a woollen mill closed down. Mr. Speaker, the total losses represented less than one per cent of capital investment in the public enterprises, which is a better record than any private consortium can show. As a matter of fact, the sodium sulphate corporation could in one year, making as it does at this time profits of between $800,000 and $900,000 a year, pay off any losses incurred in these other operations.
But profits are not the whole story; there are also the services which were provided to the public. Power rates were reduced four times consecutively. Natural gas was sold to the people of the province at 25 cents per thousand cubic feet less than any private company was prepared to charge and, in addition, communities were served which no private company was prepared to reach.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext: Per cubic foot?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext: I said 25 cents per m.c.f. less than any private company was prepared to charge.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext: Per thousand.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
In addition, there were the jobs which were provided. Investment in the public sector in Saskatchewan provided jobs at much less per employed person than is being spent today by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which is handing hundreds of millions of dollars to private corporations which are producing relatively few jobs. So, I want no more talk referring to a "a fiasco" in the Province of Saskatchewan.
What should be the purpose of the CDC? It should be used as an economic tool to do some of the things which must be done in this country, and which the present government and preceding governments have failed to do. It should first of all be used to stop the increasing takeover of Canadian corporations by foreign multinational corporations. I agree with my hon. friend from Greenwood; we are not asking the CDC to begin at this point to buy back foreign ownership. This may come in the future. The immediate task facing the government is to halt the rapid acceleration in the takeover of Canadian businesses. The CDC should be doing this. Will such a task be possible, having regard to the very limited control and narrow influence which the government will retain in this company?
Canada Development Corporation
The CDC properly constituted, should be designed to help reduce the regional disparities which are tearing this country apart. This does not mean taking industries into areas where they are bound to lose money; if we are to invest money provided by Canadian taxpayers there have to be feasibility studies, we have to make sure that industries which are established have a reasonable chance of success. But a Canadian Development Corporation, properly established, could, on the basis of the necessary studies, having decided what industries are indigenous to the area concerned, develop undertakings which private corporations have so far neglected to bring into being. A properly constituted CDC could speed up the whole process of the rationalization of industry in this country, something which is badly needed. I will not repeat the story which has been recited so often to the effect that we have developed in Canada a branch plant economy producing for a limited market. Contrast this with the achievement of a small country such as Sweden, with a population of 7 million, or Norway, with a population of 3 million. Norway and Sweden have rationalized their industry, specializing in areas which are natural to their resources and expertise, and are presently competing in the markets of the world against the industrial giants. This is what Canada must do, and it can only be done if there is an instrument of national policy which is constituted to achieve that end.
The corporation should be using the savings of the Canadian people to set up industries which will process more of our raw materials in order to provide jobs for our people and give us a better return in world markets. To my mind, this is the most important task which should face such a corporation. Everyone knows that in Canada we are shipping out our raw materials and increasingly divesting ourselves of control over our energy resources. We are shipping to the United States and to Japan the raw materials on the one hand, and the energy resources on the other, to convert our raw materials into finished products which are then sold back to us. For as long as I can remember, it has been Liberal doctrine that if only we had a favourable balance of trade Canada would be wealthy.
Well, we do have a favourable trade balance, the highest in our history. But what are we doing? We are shipping out our raw material at relatively low prices and buying back finished goods at relatively high prices. What is the result? Last year, 200,000 young people came on to the labour market and we could provide jobs for only 77,000 of them. How can we provide jobs when our whole economy is being devoted mainly to extraction industries? The government keeps saying: we need more capital. But this capital goes into the extraction industries which are capital intensive but are not labour intensive. For example, we develop a great coal industry to supply coal to Japan on the basis of automated equipment which needs relatively little manpower to run. We are shipping out iron ore, again an operation which provides relatively little employment; the employment is to be found in turning this ore into iron and into steel and, eventually, into steel products. This is the only way in

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
which we shall develop a nation; we shall not develop a nation by sitting back selling our raw materials, selling our energy resources, and committing them for years in advance.
One has only to look at what happened last fall with respect to gas. We in this party protested the fact that the government was agreeing to the export of 6.3 trillion cubic feet of gas to the United States over the next 20 years without having given adequate consideration to our own probable needs. Now, what do we find? We find that before a hearing of the National Energy Board the President of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines says: We shall have to ask our customers in eastern Canada not to demand more gas; we are completely surprised at the increased demand in a period of only five months; it has increased by 122 billion cubic feet and we cannot meet this demand. We are mortgaging our energy resources decades in advance and shipping out our raw material. Then, we wonder why we have three-quarters of a million people unemployed.
Under this bill the Canadian economy is being sold out to the corporate elite of this country. There is no guarantee that if the Canada Development Corporation puts money into a Canadian company without having majority control, that company is not going to sell out to a foreign corporation. The Canada Development Corporation will be able to do nothing about the fact that the same company that it has helped to bankroll may decide it is good business to sell out. We might as well face the fact that Canadian business has been selling out to foreign investors, and there is nothing in the bill that prevents them from continuing to sell out.
The Minister of Finance in introducing this measure on February 22 said that it was not the only thing the government intended to do to maintain Canadian ownership. But what other things does the government intend to do? We have not heard a word as to that. Certainly, this measure will not do very much to guarantee Canadian ownership of the major part of the Canadian economy. This is a sell out, not only to the corporate establishment of this country but so far as the expectations of the Canadian people are concerned.
I think the Canadian people expected when the government was talking about a Canada Development Corporation it was going to be a tool which the government would use to make sure that the vast resources of this country were developed by Canadians and for Canadians; that it would be used to expand our economy under Canadian control, to the end that this country might once again have a measure of economic independence, something that is rapidly vanishing before our eyes. Three thousand years ago a wise man said: "Where there is no vision the people perish". If this government stands accused of anything, it stands accused of lacking the vision to do something about the economic plight of Canadians. Canada is a country with more resources per capita than any nation in the world; a country not only with natural resources but with the energy resources to

convert those natural resources into consumer goods; a country with a trained labour force and managerial skill; a country which, if it were prepared to plan its economy in terms of human need, could be one of the wealthiest and happiest nations in the world.
This government had a great opportunity to forge an instrument which could be used to build a greater and finer Canada. The government has failed to seize that opportunity. Instead, it presents us with this hybrid that ensures there will be neither public ownership nor private ownership but a mixture which, though it may result in some investors making a few profits, will deprive the Canadian people of what they require, namely a government agency designed to make Canada a great nation with a great destiny, something which our forefathers envisaged but which to date we have failed to bring to fruition.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the act to
establish the Canada Development Corporation is no doubt an indication of the desire of the government to make this country's companies more Canadian. We agree of course with this principle. Its good intent must be emphasized and recognized. We have a duty, however, to criticize as objectively as possible the conditions of government action with respect to this development corporation.
The misgivings expressed by citizens of the province of Quebec will be better understood in the light of the results arrived at by a similar corporation established in Quebec a few years ago and known as the General Investment Corporation. My colleague from Compton (Mr. Latulippe) already referred to it. I shall not repeat here the arguments that he put forward.
May I nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, give the basic reasons for which, in my opinion, this act will perhaps not achieve its stated aims. First we must remember this major concept which daily experience invariably supports: the soundness of a concern and its success are based upon the work, the energy and the leadership of its members.
Now nobody can deny the necessity of a large measure of independence in the setting up of a sound company. Shareholders must feel they are competent and fully responsible. Any arbitrary and foreign control will soon paralyse all the good will in the world. Nothing is more serious than relying upon others.
I do not intend to demonstrate the viability of private enterprise as opposed to the financial problems generally encountered in state-owned enterprises, but I shall point out the basic reason why people do not work as much or as well when they know they are working for the government. Taking life easy is in style. Nobody wants to do more than the other guy, and who needs a rat race? In other words, one is less responsible when co-managing a company with the government. From which proceeds the principle that the government must provide assistance- on this we agree, Mr. Speaker-without interfering
March 2, 1971

Therefore, if we refer to the objective set forth on February 22 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), we certainly do agree, and I quote:
-help develop and maintain strong Canadian-controlled and Canadian-managed corporations in the private sector of the economy, and
-second part of that objectiveto give Canadians greater opportunities to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we all agree on this point. The question is invariably how and by what means will those purposes be achieved. And since more or less unfortunate experiences have been made, these should not be repeated.
The Minister of Finance stated in his speech on February 22nd that:
Business and industry have entered a new period of internationalism which makes it desirable that there be a number of Canadian controlled corporations with headquarters in Canada and with the kind of institutional strength and management capabilities to compete successfully in Canadian and international markets.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that in principle we agree with this, but I owe it to myself to emphasize that this hang-up about international trade, international industry, international competition, is worth just that. Some time or other, it will be necessary to revert to a more elementary, more positive, more realistic principle, which is the following: If Canada has everything required to feed and clothe its population, to improve its comfort, in short, all the required manpower to that end, and all the primary resources required, and all we need is funds, we just have to make those funds available for the distribution of goods. And in saying this, I am not merely repeating a Creditiste fad.
When the country's economy is being paralysed under the pretense that we must join the international community of nations, often we go too far in that direction. And it was no doubt in virtue of such a principle that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in New Zealand about a year ago, that we would import more dairy products from that country, and that the Canadian policy in that field aimed at a restriction of local production in order to purchase dairy products elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, if this principle were implemented, if we accept to stop producing what we were able to manufacture at the same price as in the United States, Europe, Asia, Latin America and Africa, in short, if we totally applied this principle we would have only to remain idle while importing and waiting.
We do know that this is impossible. We must not be haunted by international trade. Rather we should say: We have everything needed here to make products; let us make them. People are ready to consume them, let us give them the opportunity to do so. This is a principle of balance and sound accounting that should have been implemented long ago.
It would also be necessary, before establishing any new firm, to think of laying more stress on assistance to existing industries. In fact, there seems to be very poor
Canada Development Corporation co-ordination in the matter. Through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, we lend haphazard assistance to some firms while we seem to ignore difficulties thus created for other existing concerns.
It seems that it is not so much a matter of bad faith as of poor co-ordination and poor leadership. If certain businesses cannot progress, or even survive, owing to the insufficient purchasing power of consumers, we will not settle the problem by helping such enterprises. We should insist, and in any case this is anticipated as on February 22 the Minister of Finance spoke as follows:
The CDC would seek to achieve its first objective by investing in the equity of existing corporations, by helping in the expansion and establishment of significant new enterprises and by assisting the expansion of existing ones.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to point out that I agree with that. But, one must surely not forget existing undertakings, and one must surely not favour, through lack of co-ordination, some sort of dead-end in this field, protecting one at the expense of the other or creating a new industry at the expense of others already in existence. As a matter of fact, one must first of all see to what is already there, and help if necessary.
Mr. Speaker, one must always, in everything, naturally with regard to undertakings, in the sense that is meant in the establishment of the Canada Development Corporation, be wary of such direct action by the government. The powers that be may have the best of intentions, but the next year or a few years later, others may have taken their place and their intentions may not be quite the same, and then there may be very dire and disastrous consequences.
I disagree here with the too direct role the government intends to play in that Corporation, especially when we read at page 5 of the statement made by the Minister of Finance and I quote:
During any period when the government's voting shares exceed 50 per cent, of the outstanding shares issued, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce will be appointed ex-officiofortunately he added:
[DOT]-non-voting members of the board.
Mr. Speaker, we always look disapprovingly upon this direct action of the political members of the government in undertakings which in a sound economy should be entirely managed by Canadians, but exclusively according to the needs of the people and the spirit of initiative of those who wish to participate in the production. And when we realize that the government is considering direct action such as the minister sets out, we feel greatly reluctant. The minister goes even further when he adds in another paragraph:
Initially the government will be the sole shareholder and it will always be the largest single shareholder. Because of the significant role the corporation has been given by its purposes and objects, the government will want to show a continuing interest in it, and it is expected that the government will always want to hold at least 10 per cent of the voting shares. Thus, it will always be in a position to exercise the degree of influence on the over-all policies of the corporation which would be appropriate to its shareholding at any particular time.

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
It is clear enough that the intention is to control the Corporation through politicians in government and then-
