subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CUSTODY AND MAINTENANCE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
that Bill C-30, to amend the Divorce Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, one of the great accomplishments of the Parliament which preceded this Parliament was the act to amend the Divorce Act which was passed in 1967 and 1968. It brought progress in this important field to a country which for many years had suffered under archaic laws relating to divorce. I believe it is a law which has stood up remarkably well, even in changing times over the past three years. Perhaps I might give the reason, although it is not really germane to the debate. We know the British have again amended their divorce act in order to get rid of the so-called fault concept. I suggest to those in this House who might favour this approach that in a large measure we did that when we dealt with the three year breakup of marriage in addition to retaining some of the older fault grounds, such as adultery and cruelty.
There may be a disposition some day to take a look at the Divorce Act and perhaps move entirely away from the fault basis, but I do not believe there is really any burning need in that respect. I think our Act is good. If I were to make any suggestions in respect of improvement I would say we could bring down the cost of divorce to Canadians. A number of cases are uncontested. I suppose about half the cases really do not involve the rights of children or property rights of the husband or wife. In that situation, it seems to me there is a fearful waste of courtroom time and a fearful cost to the people who must go through a rather elaborate legal procedure when something better could be devised. However, I do not suggest that in this rather modest measure we are discussing in this particular hour. What I am suggesting is an area of correction in the present section 11 of the Divorce Act. I believe I have made my argument pretty well in the explanatory notes that accompany both suggested changes.
The first suggestion involves giving some flexibility to the judges when they are in the process of granting a decree nisi. As perhaps everyone is aware there are two stages of a divorce decree. There is the decree nisi in the first instance, followed in three months' time by the decree absolute. The decree nisi procedure is what I am concerned with here. I am concerned about this because, at a meeting in Toronto a few years ago, the judges decided that all the major issues really had to be dealt with at the decree nisi stage in view of the way Parliament had framed this particular provision. In framing it we said that the courts, upon granting a decree nisi of divorce, may do all sorts of things with regard to orders in respect of the custody and maintenance of children and the like. We really did not give the courts flexibility in that regard. I, and other lawyers, have been involved
March 2, 1971

in cases in which we found we had to wait to get the decree nisi granted because, either we had not dealt with the matter of the custody of the children at the trial or the judge wanted to hear more evidence in respect of the custody of the children. In some cases the order was found to be defective when we tried to enforce it.
The judges have found their own cure for this defect in section 11. They make one dollar orders for maintenance and then it is quite simple under the present act to amend the one dollar order to a larger amount or cut it out altogether. This is a technicality, and sometimes technicalities are the cause of a miscarriage of justice. I am aware of cases where people have been deprived of their children just because of the lack of the two little words in my bill. I suggest that when something like this happens, it is up to Parliament to make a correction.
The other suggestion I make is an equally modest one. However, it has some relevance to those Canadians who move about. This has to do with a provision for looking into an order where a person has moved from one part of Canada to another. In this large country, it is no fun trying to chase down someone and bring him into court when an order is made in a Nova Scotia court and one of the parties has moved, say, to British Columbia. Under the law as we now have it we are left really with the court of original jurisdiction. Yet this country is over 3,000 miles wide and surely we can bring about a change that would help overcome some of the geographical distance.
What I propose here is to add about a dozen or so words, which are underlined on page 2 of my bill. This would enable the court in any province where the party for whose benefit the order is made is residing to look at the original order, confirm it or order changes or variations. One of the really motivating factors which I believe brought about a change in divorce law in Canada, although for years we were sitting around with our knees sort of knocking together when we thought about the process of changing the divorce law, was the idea that we were looking after helpless people and providing for relief to be given to children. There were social injustices, but more particularly injustices involving children of marriages that had broken up and therefore Parliament had to do something about them. Yet, sir, unless we adopt the simple variation that I am suggesting here many women who have moved from one province to another with their children will experience great difficulty if they attempt to vary an order because of changed circumstances. The person has to go back to the province where the order was obtained. I think this is an injustice which can be cured by adopting the formula I propose or by adopting some other formula.
So, it is in the spirit of bringing a new broom to reach into the few musty corners that have developed under our Divorce Act of a couple of years ago that I present Bill C-30 to the House this afternoon. I hope that it, or some measure like it can be tackled reasonably soon. I do not think we have to go into a whole new debate on divorce, but we should always have some care for good
Divorce Act
housekeeping. We should spend some time during our private member's hour to cure some of the little but griping defects that crop up in our legislation from time to time. I hope that I will not bring down the heavens or a full scale, dramatic debate on divorce by simply suggesting these two small but important areas of reform.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CUSTODY AND MAINTENANCE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity-and I could say the privilege-to give marriage preparation courses for 12 years and even though I do not claim to be an expert on the question, I find the subject matter of my hon. friend's proposal quite interesting.
At the outset of my remarks, I wish to deplore the ever increasing number of divorces and the regrettable situation which is thus being created.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this intolerance between spouses, between children and their parents, is one of the causes of the problems we are facing in our modern society.
In my view, divorce is a plight, a situation which in principle should not be considered as normal. All too many people tend to consider divorce and its consequences as a normal situation and I wish to take exception to the attitude of some people for whom marriage is a situation which is not necessarily to be chosen by the majority of the people living on this planet.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that marriage is indissoluble. This should not lead anyone to conclude that I am unable to comprehend particular situations and the difficulties of some people who have chosen matrimony by interest, who have chosen to spend their lives together without first weighing the consequences of their action.
I am convinced that an adequate preparation for prospective spouses and an accepted adaptation can overcome most problems. Incompatibility of temper is undoubtedly something that can be foreseen but, what often happens is that people through self-interest or for considerations other than that of living together decide to get married.
Mr. Speaker, marriage courses are an institution that should be generalized. As a matter of fact, they are becoming more and more popular. They enable an engaged couple to know each other better and prepare themselves better for their new life. They enable individuals to realize, before it is too late, the impossibility of living together and the possibility of re-examining their choice.
Mr. Speaker, I believe one must try to face the present situation with a little more realism and that is what I will endeavour to do even after pointing out that although divorce bears the stamp of law, I believe it remains a situation that I consider, as a matter of principle, abnormal, even if I may admit that some individuals have no other alternative.
Mr. Speaker, the new Divorce Act corrects a distasteful situation. Formerly obliged to plead their case in Ottawa and to prove adultery on the part of the spouse, people from Quebec especially did not easily reconcile them-

March 2, 1971
Divorce Act
selves to divorce, but the marriage institution, one must admit, did not fare any better there than in other provinces.
We merely pretended to ignore it. Simplified as it is, divorce is nonetheless a serious decision that is far from amusing. A love story ending amidst the gloomy setting of a court is nothing to be envied.
An act likely to weaken the family, the basic unit in our society, and involving serious consequences for two adult people and their children, must, first of all, be scrutinized. It is worth knowing all about the divorce machinery and trying to learn what becomes of the individuals concerned, in such a case of permanent separation.
However, in divorce, the women are the losers. First, there are four times as many women as men available in this country; besides, because they look after the children, women accept heavy responsibilities, morally and materially. There is all the difference in the world between taking two children out on Sunday afternoon and looking after them each day of the year, answering all their questions, facing their emotional problems, explaining to a young daughter why her father is not always there, as her little girl-friend's father.
Mr. Speaker, in Quebec the family has been for some years submitted to tremendous pressures which are leaving it shaken to its very foundations. Social changes and new ideologies have both contributed to reduce significantly its traditional importance. The role of the family is different now. Contacts between its members are not so frequent and generally not so rewarding.
Even though these facts may be explained, it remains that the family is now undergoing a delicate period of adjustment. It should also be recognized that a couple's life, mainly in the cities, has become harder. Formerly marriage had a precise meaning for all Catholics. A man and a woman got married for better or worse without worrying too much about a possible separation if the worst was to overcome the best.
The Divorce Act no doubt reflects a weaker religious faith. This act has changed everything. In 1971, when serious difficulties are met, the spouses are very much tempted to resort to the final solution. In this context, perhaps we should not be surprised at the bishops' statement who deplore the present situation of the Quebec family.
The document issued by the Canadian and Quebec episcopate on the occasion of its quarterly meeting is quite clear. Among the events which influenced our people's way of thinking is the provincial legislation which permits marriage before a civil officer and mainly the federal legislation which multiplied the reasons for civil divorce and its implementation in Quebec courts.
To say that the bishops cannot but condemn divorce would be quite easy. The problems created by divorce for the spouses and the children are real and recent statistics are worth considering. From July 1, 1968 to September 9, 1970, 11,030 civil divorce cases were recorded in Montreal and 1,817 in Quebec.

When the law was implemented, it was believed that the number of divorces would decline after the first year. Now, after more than two years, requests for civil divorce continue to increase at an alarming rate. Each month, requests number about 500 at the Montreal record office-at the end of 1970 yet.
In their pastoral letter, bishops avoided denouncing directly the law authorizing divorce but did mention its serious consequences. Under the circumstances, they were right in asking the state to formulate and apply a policy likely to prevent family problems which prompt married couples to divorce.
The suggestion of my hon. friend comprises two points. The first is concerned with adding words which, in some way, would allow the court or the judge who will grant a decree nisi not to rule immediately on the matter of alimony or custody of the children. In the present situation, upon granting a decree nisi of divorce, the judge may, if he thinks it fit, and having regard to the circumstances, make an order requiring the husband to secure or to pay such lump sum or sums owing to the wife or the children.
I do not believe that the proposal of my hon. friend is acceptable, not because the judges have already expressed the opinion that it would not be advisable not to make such an order at the same time as the decree nisi, but simply because while hearing divorce cases, it is desirable that the debate be decided at the same time, and that the judge who must decide whether or not a divorce is advisable, may at the same time render a decision as to alimony and custody.
It seems essential to me that the judge who must decide to grant the divorce or not be empowered also to render a judgment on those important matters of alimony and custody. It would be a mistake, I think, to try and separate the two questions, since divorce invariably brings about the problem of the custody of the children. And if a judge, for some reason or other, had to decide on a divorce and not on the custody of children at the same time, truly abnormal and irregular situations could arise which would eventually be detrimental to the children. And the most important thing to be decided in these cases is not so much the divorce but the implications it bears for the children.
I suggest then that my hon. friend's proposal, although I do not deem it ridiculous-on the contrary, it makes some sense-is not at all desirable.
As far as the second proposal of my hon. friend is concerned, it seems quite justified to me at first sight. When two people get a divorce in one province and if the person in whose favour the divorce has been granted leaves that province afterwards, there might be practical difficulties involved for the person wishing to go to court again because of the distance and the different circumstances in which that person may be. The financial implications for anyone who has had a divorce in Quebec and who would be residing in British Columbia might well prevent her from obtaining justice for herself and
March 2, 1971

for her children if due to the circumstances she were justified in requesting a change in alimony or new arrangements for the custody of the children.
Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to say whether from a constitutional point of view this would involve insuperable difficulties. However, I would simply like to say that at first sight, the suggestion made by my hon. friend seems fair and reasonable and it would be easy to propose some amendments to the act that would help solve this problem.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, allow me to say this: There can be no substitute for personal individual effort. It is the duty of every Christian to carry out fully the values of his marriage commitments.
Christian parents are to give their children the example of a union lived in faith and love; that is one of their responsibilities, and an irreplaceable one.
A sound preparation should reveal to future spouses that the depth of their mutual commitment will ensure their faithfulness.
Judges and lawyers, as the law requires of them, should give positive assistance to people in view of reconciliation, informing them, if necessary, of agencies and means available to help them.
All agencies involved in family problems should unite their efforts and co-operate actively in order to avoid dispersal of available resources and I am aware of the tremendous work they have already accomplished.
It is the state's duty to develop and apply policies likely to prevent the evils we have referred to. We cannot but support here what many others have already been calling for: the establishment of a "family court". The concrete terms of the organization and operation of such a court are the work of experts. They will no doubt find a source of inspiration in existing organizations.
I hope that this court will be able to solve distressing familial problems in a more simple way than presently.
Family problems in modern society are acute. I hope that, all together, we shall have the courage to face them and find efficient solutions in keeping with today's world.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CUSTODY AND MAINTENANCE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to follow the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) who has eloquently dealt with the bill before the House. I think that the bill presented by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) has a great deal of merit, particularly in respect of new section 11(1). As we know, the evidence in divorce cases is usually prepared thoroughly yet often the parties are ill-prepared to consider the welfare of the children; therefore the trial judge cannot easily dispose of this matter. The trial judge also faces difficulties respecting alimony and support.
New section 11(1) contains the words "or after" and the first part of it reads:
Upon or alter granting a decree nisi of divorce, the court :may, if it thinks it fit and just-
Divorce Act
And so on. If the evidence respecting the children has not been properly prepared, and if the parties have not been as careful and as frank as they ought to have been regarding that evidence, the judge in my opinion ought not to be hasty in making a custody order. In such cases he might make a serious error.
We must consider several matters if the court is to be given the power not only of deciding on divorce but also on the children of the marriage, as is proposed in this bill. In Ontario there is an office known as the official guardian. The official guardian is an officer of the court and employs welfare officers who investigate the cases of children concerned. They are supposed to do their jobs thoroughly. Sometimes they do not do so. I submit it would be wrong for us to say that the divorce ought to be delayed merely because a careful judge-and most judges are careful-considers that the report of the welfare officer is fragmentary and he is suspicious that one or more of the children is being neglected.
I say by all means let the divorce go through, but allow the court to determine the issue of custody after there has been care and preparation in bringing forward the evidence. I regret that in some provinces there is no official guardian to investigate the welfare of the children concerned. I hope that all provinces will take this great step forward which is so necessary if one is to look into the welfare of children. I firmly believe that in the matter of custody the welfare of the child is paramount. Before I deal with the second matter raised in the bill- and it raises many interesting points-I should like to read proposed new section 11(2):
An order made pursuant to this section may be varied from time to time or rescinded by the court that made the order or by the court for any province where the party for whose benefit the order was made is residing if it thinks it fit to do so having regard to the conduct of the parties since the making of the order or any change in the condition, means or other circumstances of either of them.
Let us suppose that the husband is awarded custody of two children by an Ontario court and he and the children are living in Ontario. Then the wife moves to British Columbia and before moving, pursuant to the Ontario judge's order, obtains access to the children for two weeks. She moves to British Columbia and the children go with her. Then let us suppose that the wife becomes ill, needs assistance in supporting the children and cannot get them back to Ontario. I submit that in this case the husband would be in difficulties. Which court would have jurisdiction over the children? I maintain that in order to safeguard the welfare of the children the province in which they normally reside ought to have jurisdiction.
The circumstances I have outlined would create great difficulties for the parents. Is the wife to be permitted to go to the British Columbia Supreme Court and obtain an order for the children? She may not be a fit and proper person to have their custody. And what is to happen to the husband who is in Ontario? He might apply to the Ontario court for an order to enforce his rights provided in the original judgment. Which order is to prevail?

The hon. member's bill contains the germ of a good idea. I do not wish to throw mud on his proposal because it heads in the right direction. We recognize, in other words, that people move. When they move, their circumstances sometimes change. We must therefore find a way of dealing with conflicts created by modern times. I commend the hon. member for his thoughtfulness, yet I am afraid that his suggestion will not do in its present form. Two fighting parents could use this law to prevent the course of true justice. Supposing the original Ontario court order provided alimony for the wife of $300 a month: if the wife moved to British Columbia and obtained an order for $500 a month, which of the two court orders would prevail? This section does not make provision for that situation. Perhaps we should give paramountcy in financial matters-that is, alimony to the court where the original order was made. In matters of custody, paramountcy should be given to the court having jurisdiction where the children reside. In any event, we are plagued today with a mobile population, difficulties of communication, difficulties of finance and all the other matters that weigh on the problems of broken homes and these unfortunate people.
The rights of the children must be strictly and zealously guarded by more up to date Children's Aid Society reporting and more skilled and conscientious social workers being brought into this problem. There are signs of this being done. I think that Ontario has a reasonably good family court system; it is improving all the time. With the young offenders legislation and statutes like it which I hope will be before the House soon, we will improve our discipline of children. On the matter of reorganization of the courts, great consideration is being given to granting county court judges jurisdiction over divorce. I hope that these judges will maintain, under the surrogate court act of Ontario, jurisdiction over the custody of infants.
Perhaps the county court judge is better fitted in many ways to deal with divorce, custody, alimony and problems of broken homes. He is in some ways a little closer to the people in the sense that he lives in the community and is not a roving judge as are the trial judges of many of our supreme courts. Perhaps the criteria should be that the county wherein the parties reside should have paramount jurisdiction over custody, and the court granting the original alimony order should be the one to decide on problems of alimony and financial questions.
This is a very interesting problem. Divorce reform has moved forward rapidly. I can honestly say that the cases I have heard about in my area have not created a flood of abusive types of divorce. Many people who were unfortunately separated and whose marriages were completely sundered have been able to obtain a divorce without adultery being the only ground. From what I have heard there has not been a flood of divorces in the sense that every second or third family is rushing to get one. I think the bona fides of the situation have been well received by the community at large.

By and large we have progressed a great distance toward more humane laws. We have failed in respect of the problems raised by section 11(2) because that section presents a technical barrier to justice-conflicting jurisdictions; which court shall have power. It is our duty and responsibility to struggle with any technical problem as to which court has power. I think the only forum wherein this problem can be solved is a federal-provincial conference. Perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Premiers of the provinces should study the matter and establish throughout Canada a uniform jurisdictional system for divorce, alimony and custody. I think that would be useful and, in light of what my hon. friend indicated, I believe he would like to see it come about.
The judge should not be pressured in a situation where he has very little evidence. He should not be forced to decide divorce and custody issues as well as financial matters if the evidence is not there. We can be almost certain that evidence as to the breakdown of the marriage will be there. There are problems in the far north, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. These areas were visited by the Committee on the Constitution. There were complaints that spouses had moved many hundreds of miles away and there was no way of obtaining speedy justice. I hope this Parliament will seek ways to improve the system of helping people in remote parts of Canada to obtain speedier and less costly relief than at present. Many people in the far north are unable to receive speedy justice. Their children are in the same boat. We should have a legal aid system which will assist, in particular, the children of broken marriages in the far north.
I commend the mover of this bill. I cannot agree with the details of section 11(2) but I think it is a very thoughtful and interesting proposal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House is of particular interest to the first society that ever existed on this planet-mankind.
If I correctly understand the origin of man on earth, the family is of divine institution and constitutes the foundation of our society. Even though according to what we were taught, society has been established by God, it is nonetheless made of human beings, therefore subject to imperfection. At times difficulties arise between people who were married when they were really in love but who, owing to such difficulties, have reached the point where governments have authorized the breaking up of their marriage in order to enable them to have a new start in life, if possible and if they so desire.
The bill before us provides for a change which deserves careful consideration, as we are indeed placed before an accomplished fact.
Divorce was sanctioned by civil legislation. It happens that divorces are recognized by judicial powers. Following these divorces, the family, the children, have to face problems.
I have just read an amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to the effect that the bill should be referred to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I think that this suggestion is useful. Indeed, we cannot allow ourselves to consider lightly a bill with such a wide scope and we must take all necessary means to assure that the children issued from more or less successful marriages which are finally dissolved will see their rights recognized by society, in order that they can lead a normal life.
Mr. Speaker, I think that such a question should be duly referred to a committee for thorough consideration and report and this would allow us to lessen the effects of divorce while those infortunate families and children who have to suffer from their parents' divorce could take advantage of the protection to which they are entitled and lead a normal life in our society.

It is clear that a number of improvements could be made to the law.

The second provision of the bill before us attempts to deal with the situation in which one of the parties to a marriage takes up residence in another province of Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great many words uttered on the subject of the Canada Development Corporation. A great many members who said they agreed with the principle of the bill nevertheless wondered how it might work in practice when it came down in realistic terms to financing and to human personalities. Many aspects of the bill that could be questioned and many of the fears people have of this type of legislation have already been outlined; indeed, my leader, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), expressed them very thoroughly this afternoon.
I do not propose to belabour the reasons why this bill will not work. I must say I have a certain amount of agreement with the principle of the bill even though in practice it will be completely impractical because of the personal conflicts that will make the legislation unworkable. But in looking at a measure such as this I do not believe you can oppose it absolutely without putting forward some reasonable alternative.
I am not going to attempt to cover the ground already traversed by other speakers in the debate during the past week or so. This afternoon the leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), expressed some concern over foreign ownership in Canada and contended that we should process our natural resources here in Canada, thus creating more jobs and industries which would, if not wholly, at least partially solve our unemployment problem.
To my mind the important thing is not where the ownership of corporate entities lies; it is more a matter of how the capital and the profits made by these corporations are employed once the corporations are created. I believe this boils down to the philosophy of wanting the state to go into the business of manufacturing goods, creating wealth in this country and then distributing it to each individual according to his need. I do not believe the state should be involved in this sort of thing. Rather than the state looking after all things for all men, manufacturing goods and distributing them to each according to his need, I believe an alternative solution can be worked out.
I support the philosophy that the individual is paramount and that the main role of government is, in addition to keeping the peace and maintaining national security, the development and maintenance of a social, economic and political climate in which the individual can achieve his or her fulfilment. As an alternative to the doctrine of socialism, where the state takes all and distributes to each according to his need, we must recognize that in a technological society such as ours, the capital instruments of production-the machines and devices that produce-are rapidly supplanting labour as the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Richard).]
major producer of wealth. We should also recognize that there are only three ways in which an individual can support himself and his dependents: by his own labour power, by the earning power of his capital or by a combination of both. It should be the policy in the future to encourage and facilitate by every means possible the widest possible individual ownership of capital, particularly the ownership of common or equity shares in our many well established companies.
I support this idea, and in this vein I want to read to the House some remarks made by Mr. Frank Capon, vice-president and director of Dupont of Canada Limited in a speech he made at St. Louis, Missouri:
We have come full circle. Originally, security was based on-ownership of land, which was capital. Today, security can come only from the ownership of the machines which produce incomes, which is still capital. Unfortunately, we allowed ourselves to get trapped in a fallacy that it was labour, or the human element, that produced the goods of the industrial revolution and that job security was therefore a legitimate and, in fact, vital right of the citizen. We must now make the choice. Either we recognize that most wealth is, and always was, produced by capital and that the security which is an innate need of the human animal can be satisfied only by ensuring a broad ownership of capital amongst our households. Or we will hold stubbornly to the concept that wages are the proper basis for wealth distribution, that job security is essential, that workers have the right to stop our whole economy short as they strike to enforce demands, and that the state will finally "guarantee" to all an income above the "poverty" level.
It is precisely because we are still on the latter course that we see the upsurge of irresponsible wage increases, the dramatic growth in strikes particularly against the community as a whole rather than against individual employers, and the inevitable destruction of our currency values by inflation. Already, interest rates have been pushed to historic highs, endangering the ability to finance government and industrial needs by bonds which are a cornerstone of our entire structure. The tolerance of all our people against hardship, poverty and unemployment was never lower, because they have been assured that we now have the ability to create affluence and that governments can be relied on to give them guaranteed incomes. In desperation youth, coloured people, unionized workers, and even school teachers turn to violence in their frustration at the absence of any effective leadership in the solution of our basic dilemma. Man must have security, even if in the final analysis it is only the security of knowing that everyone is in equally desperate straits.
We must look at the situation and recognize the fact that if we are going to perpetuate the free enterprise system as an alternative to socialism, we must design some method of increasing capital ownership and capitalists in this country. This is very basic to the direction we are heading today. I repeat, if we continue to follow the direction we are following today, we must think in terms of creating more capitalists in Canada. We must ensure that more individuals become owners of the common and preferred stock of established companies.
An alternative to socialism as proposed is the establishment of a type of insurance company or consortium of companies to ensure individual and group loans to Canadians by existing financial institutions in order to buy newly issued common stocks of publicly listed Canadian companies. I suggest that one precedent for this would be insured house mortgages under the National Housing Act, with government backing.
March 2, 1971

I suggest that it might be possible to use the ten blue chip stocks in Canada-those companies that have the best growth performance in this country-in order to ensure this type of investment. If we look to the performance of our ten top Canadian companies I suggest it would be much easier to guarantee these stocks than it would be the stocks of individual houses. One does not know the type of ownership he will get in respect of a house, in stock terms. To use the terminology of the range, it is easier to kick hell out of a house than it is to kick hell out of a house financed by ownership stock. This should be borne in mind. It would necessitate amendment to the Income Tax Act to exempt from corporate income tax the new common stock issues that companies issue to finance their corporate expansions, provided that all earnings, less depreciation and other approved allowances, were paid out to the new stockholders.
This would enable the new stockholders who have borrowed the money to buy stocks to repay their loans and the interest thereon from the earnings of the stocks rather than from their own pockets. There is some precedence for this. I refer to the rapid depreciation that is now being allowed in respect of plants being built in designated areas.
I believe when we look at the earnings of the top ten companies in Canada we will see there is a net earnings picture, before tax, of something between 16 per cent and 33 per cent. From the evidence in the United States it would seem that 90 per cent of the capital expansion of companies comes from late earnings, and 10 per cent from new share issues. I suggest that if these companies were to pay out to the shareholders the 90 per cent they now retain and finance their capital expansion through new shareholdings, it would be possible for all the basic participants in industry to get a part of the action. Obviously, loans will be insured only for the purchase of new common stocks approved by the insuring company. I think this would cover most of the new stock issues of most mature Canadian companies.
I suggest, in order to prevent what we might term the greedy taking advantage of this socially desirable situation, the purchase of such stock by individuals should be limited to perhaps $2,000 per year per adult up to a certain date each year, and that thereafter the individual's limit be progressively raised until all the new issue is purchased. The companies whose stocks are not approved by the insuring companies of course will have to be financed in the conventional way.
I hate at this time, because of the present situation, to refer to the growth trend of companies but I should like to refer to the pre-Benson days when things were running along normally in this country and the businessmen did not have the wits, as we might say, scared out of them. I could refer to the growth of the economy in Japan, as an example. The growth of Japan is probably the most dynamic in the world today. The Japanese economy has been expanding since World War II, for the last 20 or 25 years, at an average rate of more than 9 per
Canada Development Corporation
cent per year. I think it was only last year that it reached something like 13 per cent. Practically all this growth has been financed internally in Japan.
I suggest that the situation in Japan bears looking at. I see no reason why we could not create the same type of performance here in Canada, with the type of country and people we have. I do not think what I am suggesting can be brought about overnight; I believe it would probably take a decade or more to accomplish it. However, if we could establish the policy of a second income, I believe this would automatically reduce one of the many problems we have today. I refer to such things as welfare and strikes. In this way the factory workers would participate in industry, would be shareholders in industry and would feel they were part of the situation.
There are a great many government hand-outs in the society we have today, but I say again a permanent solution cannot be found in the present method of redistributing wealth, which I suppose is based on what we might term the Robin Hood principle of plundering some to give to others. In addition to plundering some to give to others, we have the government stealing from us all through inflation. This is a continual process. No one can deny that these factors are present. We are witnessing this every day, and it is growing.
In contrast, the suggestion I have made is based upon the principle of helping our people become self-supporting by participating in the economy both as workers and owners. Under these conditions I think we would find that social strife would reduce rapidly because people would be more content to do their own thing. I do not believe they would be continually attempting to get a bigger piece of a limited economic cake by means of coercion by government, by groups and by labour unions. I am suggesting that anybody in this House who believes in the principle of free enterprise, and who believes that the government should not merely take over and distribute everything, would agree-when I say everybody, I include all parties in this House-that we should see that the workers have a piece of the action. We have to make more capitalists in this country. I sincerely believe this is the only alternative to what might ultimately become a completely socialist state.

speechtext:
It is for this reason we have suggested that the House, through the instrumentality of one of its committees, examine what is proposed in light of certain information. We know that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) will, shortly we hope, be bringing before the House and the country a report dealing with the whole vexed and difficult question of the national ownership of our resources. There is a real problem here. We recognize it; all the speakers from this side of the House have said so. My leader stated it categorically this afternoon. We want the remedy to be an appropriate one and applied in the light of proven, established facts. We do not yet have those facts. We want them before we continue with this bill. This is why the Leader of the Opposition suggested that an amendment at the present time could profitably be put forward.
After all, this is not only a Canadian problem; it is a world problem. It has arisen in the United Kingdom and in all the countries of Europe. The other day I was reading in the last issue of the World Federalist an interesting article entitled "The multinational corporation." Before I move the amendment I should like to read part of this article as follows:
No scheme of world order can afford to neglect either the enormous power controlled by the multinational corporations, or the special problems created both by the artificial nationality of each corporation and by the real national citizenship of the individual members of its managerial elite.
The first step in dealing with this problem is to recognize the reality that exists-the condition of anarchy, in which each multinational corporation is very largely a law unto itself. This reality was succinctly stated by the Barber commission (a Canadian royal commission study of prices of farm machinery) :
"These multinational corporations are independent of the national authority of individual countries. At the present time no international authority exists which can exercise control over them."
The article suggests three approaches, and I deal with this because it becomes apparent that the issue we are considering is not one which is peculiar to us; intellectuals, academics and politicians all over the world, particularly in the west, are deeply concerned about it. Here are the suggestions which are made in this article:
A supranational organization, an agency of the United Nations might be established with three branches:
(a)	A legislative branch which would work out by negotiation between the interested parties, experts acting for the

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
corporations themselves, other experts acting on behalf of the nations permitting the export of capital, and still. others representing nations permitting foreign investment within their territories, a comprehensive set of rules. These rules would make conditions uniform and predictable for the transfer of capital and skills across international boundaries, and from one jurisdiction to another.
(b) The judicial branch, expanded from the machinery provided in the 1966 Convention for the Settlement of Investment Disputes, would provide impartial third party judgment to settle disputes and thereby establish precedents for the avoidance of similar disputes in the future
(c) An administrative and audit branch to license the operation of world corporations agreeing to conform in their operations to the rules laid down by the legislative branch, and to submit to the jurisdiction of the panels of experts set up under the judicial branch; to audit and supervise the accounts of the world corporations, to collect taxes to cover the cost of these operations and to provide revenue for the United Nations.
I do not accept this approach in its totality, but I quote the article to support my contention that this issue is one which is engaging the attention of many people in the world and that for us to rush through the kind of inadequate legislation placed before us at this time, without knowledge of the facts which will be brought before the House in the various reports mentioned in my amendment, would be absolute nonsense. While accepting the principle that something needs to be done, we say: Let us wait until we have the facts, and then act. With this as notice for the amendment, I move, seconded by my hon. friend from South Shore (Mr. Crouse):
That all the words after "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Bill C-219 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, together with the eighteenth report of that committee in the previous session on the white paper on tax reform and such report, if any, as may be tabled in this session, on the inquiry by the Minister of National Revenue into foreign investment in Canada".
Your Honour will have noted with great interest that the amendment adds somewhat to the traditional form which has been accepted in the past. We wish to make demonstrably plain the precise terms of the material we want the committee to cover. If, however, there should be some doubt in Your Honour's mind as to the acceptability of the amendment in this form, I will be prepared to omit the last words so that there will be no problem at all in connection with the amendment.

The hon. member will appreciate that there are serious procedural difficulties about the form of the proposed amendment. The hon. member admitted he was aware of the difficulties. They relate to the second part of the amendment. He seeks to import into the consideration that would be given by the committee matters such as the eighteenth report of the committee dealing with the white paper on tax reform. This part of the amendment would hardly be acceptable from the point of view of relevancy.
I understood earlier today from remarks made in the course of debate that a reasoned amendment would be
introduced. This is, of course, not a reasoned amendment. The hon. member himself indicated that he did not propose to move an amendment which would oppose the principle of the bill, which is the essence of a reasoned amendment. I do not want to belabour the point. The hon. member said that having made the intent of his motion clear, he would be prepared to abide by the traditional form and be satisfied if the amendment were to read as follows, and I will put it formally, subject to the assent of the hon. member:
That all the words after "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Bill C-219 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs".
The hon. member indicates that he is satisfied with the amendment being put to the House in this form.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of his remarks the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said that this bill was serving no useful purpose. I think it is serving a useful purpose. As such, it is uniting people in the opposition against the government's bill. It must be an indication of how irrational is the government today when the Conservative and New Democratic parties alike, for their own reasons, can see little good in it.
A reading of the bill makes obvious why this is so. The bill does not make any sense. It does not make any sense in setting up a body to do something that the private sector could do well and in some cases is doing well on its own. Neither does it make sense in terms of setting up an organization that should be within the jurisdiction of the public sector as an instrument of government policy. That is why we have run into this situation. Obviously, the government has found itself in a bind as a result of a promise it made many years ago. It hoped to avoid keeping its promise but found that it could not do so because of public pressure. Therefore it brought in a "nothing" bill, a bill about which no one can be enthusiastic. All that this bill will do is unite public opinion in Canada against it.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) because the government wants the bill creating the CDC to be passed for two reasons.
Firstly, they want to help to maintain and develop strong private Canadian companies. Those are not the companies in need of assistance, but those which are on the verge of bankruptcy.
Secondly, through the establishment of the CDC, they would like to multiply the investment prospects in the field of economic development for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the return on investments made by the CDC will have to be competitive and proportionate to the risk, since its shares will be sold to the public at large.
The government wants the distribution of shares to be as wide as possible among Canadian citizens. Thus shares

March 2, 1971

will be sold to Canadian citizens only, and nobody will be allowed to own more than 3 per cent of voting shares.
I should like to analyse this. In the beginning, the outlay of the government of Canada will be $250 million and the capitalization will be $2 billion. It is anticipated that the first sale of equity shares to the public will be at a price of approximately $5 per share. As the government will always be the major shareholder, it will keep at least 10 per cent of the voting shares. The CDC will not be a crown corporation or department, but a company which will operate basically under the Canada Corporations Act. It will be managed by a board of 18 to 21 directors and the government will have a choice between naming not more than four of them or exercizing the voting right of its shares with regard to the complete list of directors.
Speaking of the CDC, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said in substance:
No other Canadian corporation has as its objectives national interest and profits.
Such a premise is false and I am going to prove it. He also added the following nauseating statement:
The national interest and the profit motive are not always compatible.
May I point out to the minister that these two objectives rarely go together. I fully agree that the companies and their control must remain Canadian and I think the government has made another blunder in trying to achieve an impossible balance between the two objectives mentioned by the Minister of Finance, by resorting to a socialization of the Canadian capital.
Mr. Speaker, if the national interest is to be truly advocated, then the best way of solving the problem would be to pass legislation with respect to the monetary system. If, on the contrary, one wishes to make a profit, the private sector is much more competent than the public sector, as evidenced by the failure of Crown corporations managed by the government.
A mixture like that proposed by the minister will not solve any problem, but it will have all the disadvantages of both the public and the private sector. So why should we establish the CDC? They say that the CDC will remain completely outside politics and that the federal government will not interfere with that organization.
The minister maintains that according to Bill C-219 the federal government will have the choice of either appointing a maximum of four administrators or having a voting right corresponding to the number of its shares.
If the number of shares held by the government gives it voting right exceeding 50 per cent of the number of all shares issued, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce will be appointed to the board but without a voting right.
Mr. Speaker, these provisions are supposedly intended to establish the necessary degree of additional co-ordination between the Corporation and the government, during the initial phase of its existence. It is added, however, that the Corporation will need some degree of independence so that it may reach efficiently its objectives.
Canada Development Corporation
But the government will always want-as is its habit- to hold at least 10 per cent of the voting shares in order to be able to exercice on the global policy of the Corporation the influence corresponding to its shares.
However, the Minister of Finance states that he will not involve himself in politics. The control he exercises, provides him with one more device for selling his tough policy to Canadians.
Since Bill C-219 outlines the Corporation's method of financing, the government will need strong control powers, and that is what the government wants.
Mr. Speaker, it is intended to offer common stock to the public at a price of about $5 per share, in order to encourage wide distribution of shares throughout Canada. That means it is hoped that Canadians who have never invested before will now do so. Those people are not really capitalists, accustomed to risks and therefore to losses, but rather workers, labourers, who will invest not because they hope to be reimbursed by the government, or the Corporation as a financial entity, but because such shares will be guaranteed by the government.
In this way, savings will be tapped, the purchasing power of Canadians will be reduced and, consequently, the gap between the rich and the poor will be widened. For these people, it is not, as it should be, a question of investing in the future development of a great country, but of investing in a company whose shares are guaranteed by the federal government. In acting in this way, Mr. Speaker, the government discourages people, because it is tapping those savings and that capital. It is preventing Canadians from investing personally in this country in which they believe.
It is a new and disguised form of Canada savings bonds. Whatever the Minister of Finance may say, the Canada Development Corporation will always be, judging by its shareholders, similar to a Crown corporation, and the government, politically, will never allow the Canada Development Corporation to sustain a loss in order to protect the national interest. And therein lies the dilemma.
Should such a situation ever come up and it is bound to come owing to the conflict between the national interest and the profit motive, the CDC will have no function to perform. At the present time each investor seeks profits. He does not need any government enterprise to find profitable investments, and companies liable to pay dividends to their shareholders will not need any capital from the cdc.
So in trying to protect the national interest the Canadian Development Corporation will be a failure. The businesses in need of its capital will not get it because they are not profitable at the present time. They will be sold to foreign interests, financed by private capital which can sustain an initial loss in order to make future profits.
As the government will be politically involved in the CDC, it will be unable to sustain a loss at the start in order to make profits later.

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
Mr. Speaker, the avowed purpose of the government in setting up the CDC is merely a political one, of course, especially in this period of our economic history when unemployment has reached a peak. The government will have to underwrite the shares and investments of the Corporation shareholders, because if the investors lose confidence in the CDC, they will lose confidence in the government. This is another reason why it will be a political organization.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, all Canadian taxpayers will be shareholders of the Corporation, since the government will hold at least 10 per cent of the CDC shares and will levy the necessary funds from the Canadian taxpayers, so that they will be forcibly involved in a socialist scheme. And this, under the disguised form of the party now in office.
So state socialism is imposed upon us. The government is interfering in another sector of Canadian life in a disguised and dishonest manner because it does not define both sides of the issue as it should. Thus, each decrease in the price of shares will be a loss for the government and, consequently, for each Canadian and it will be put down as a national liability, that is the liability of each Canadian.
From what I have just said, it is easy to see that each consecutive government will have to impose a strict control over the activities of the CDC, a control that will go far beyond its power according to the percentage of shares it holds. It is a matter of political survival and once again we have to conclude that the hon. Minister of Finance, through the CDC, wants to throw dust in the eyes of Canadians to make them forget the fundamental problem of the present economic unbalance.
As I have just said, the Canadian industry and economy are being and will continue to be increasingly controlled by two great powers: the Americans and the central government. The private sector will hang between the two, threatened with extinction, because it will have to compete. I refer to the large and small Canadian investors who will be squeezed between foreign investments and the taxing power of the government which, in its white paper on tax reform, discourages profits and growth in that sector of our economy. Consequently, it is an underhanded but sure way of taking it over and socializing it, as was the case with the Farm Credit Corporation, the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation and all the programs of the government which tend to "lure each citizen" into repayment plans if he wishes to become an owner.
Mr. Speaker, those control programs were always dealing with the national interest and not with profitability; naturally, this has been realized. If we really wanted to protect the Canadian industry, we would not confine ourselves strictly to that criterium of profit and we would be much more interested in national values. I am surprised to realize upon reading the speech of the Minister of Finance that all along, he thought only about his political future, the future of his party, and that he forgot the future of Canadians.
There is still a way to solve that problem, which the government has not often used. It is a program of allow-

ances or subsidies given directly to the company in order to protect those who do not want to sell their concern but who are compelled to do so because of their financial situation.
But instead of rescuing borderline companies, the government will endeavour to take over the larger companies and let the smaller sink, with the hope that both will disappear for the benefit of foreign interests or of the government. In doing so, companies which are squeezed between these two sectors are placed in the same situation as the individual who has to rely on welfare. Indidentally, an ever increasing number of companies apply for grants to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion just as a citizen will go to the welfare office to pick up his handout.
This is the situation we are in, Mr. Speaker, and not only will the CDC not solve this problem, but it will increase it by depriving these companies of the capital they require.
Mr. Speaker, such a system would be similar to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion's program-and this can be easily demonstrated-except that it would be managed by only one corporation and not necessarily in a specific area. This system could be designed to protect industry instead of letting it be overtaken by foreigners; but there is no government program to assist these industries indeed, they are being left aside while we are dealing with bigger and smaller corporations. The big ones we will own, and the smaller ones will be wiped off.
We could also provide that all newly established corporations should have a given percentage of Canadian ownership; we could also restrict the sale of shares to foreign interests since some foreign capital is always necessary.
In any way, in the light of this brief survey which I honestly attempted to submit, I believe that the CDC will never work out but as an instrument of the federal government's policy and I find this very sad for we are here precisely to give Canadians instruments to help them build their own country.
This legislation will also be a policy instrument serving the federal government because Canada is now more than ever in need of a concrete policy to deal with the program of Canadian control of industry since the main requirement in this field is national interest. In view of these factors, however, this bill merely amounts to a poultice on a wooden leg. After all these surveys, we shall wonder whether, by passing Bill C-219, we shall actually settle the question. If we really want to face reality, we shall realize that we are bogged down in the system, that this is just some dust in the eyes of Canadians and that the problem has not been dealt with properly.
The participation of every Canadian citizen to the economic life of this country is necessary. Each Canadian should be given a chance to really participate, of his own valition, freely and safely to the development and progress of this country or to its building.
March 2, 1971

Through the passing of bills such as this one, we go after Canadian capital, we undermine the savings of the Canadian people and we make them overlook the real problem. In fact, we merely reduce the purchasing power of the ordinary citizens, workers, laborers, farmers, parents, students, to the benefit of big companies and the government.
Thus the Minister of Finance says at the end of the year: Our budget has increased. Of course! With money coming from the pockets of the Canadian people, it is easy to increase one's pile; but one forgets that it behooves the government to make that money available to the Canadian people. That is one thing. Our taxation system must be reformed, but not by discouraging Canadian enterprise, as the white paper of the Minister of Finance is doing by saying on the one hand that it wants to help the corporations and on the other hand, by discouraging them and bringing about their disappearance.
The second reform-and the most important one-that must be brought about to put order in this country should be a monetary one, so that instead of implementing plans and still more plans and putting poultices on wooden legs, like the CDC, would do, we should give ourselves monetary tools with real effects on Canada's economic life, give each citizen the tool he needs to invest in the Canadian economy.
Let us not ask Canadians to invest in the CDC or somewhere else in Canada if they cannot even provide for themselves. And considering the fact that more than 45 per cent of the Quebec unemployed are less than 25 years old, one can easily understand that they cannot invest in the CDC and that the CDC is unable to cope with their problem. To be honest, one must recognize that more than 35 per cent of the Canadian people live *out of public funds, especially federal funds. Those people are excluded from the economic life of this country and do not have a single cent to invest in the CDC or anywhere else. What is being done about those people? They are being forgotten and no bill is passed for them.
We are being presented Bill C-219 to encourage Canadians to invest. But who shall invest in this corporation? Those already well-off and well-to-do. The government will hold 10 per cent of the shares. This means that it will oblige our citizens to invest in this corporation.
Now we ask this question: What will be the profit margin? The profit of the well-to-do will be quite considerable, that of the small shareholders will be minimal.
Mr. Speaker, the taxpayer who can barely pay his taxes and cannot afford to embark freely in this sytem will get zero plus zero which is zero. The well-to-do who will freely choose to invest in this corporation and to buy shares will make a profit once again at the expense of the small savings and of each Canadian. Once more the Canadian government will have cheated Canadians by showing them the fine picture that the CDC is and not telling them that by creating the CDC the low income citizens are swindled out of their money for the benefit .of the well-to-do.
Canada Development Corporation
The socialists will say: let us take from the big ones and give to the small ones! But in so doing the problem is not solved since our economic system will keep on producing big ones and small ones. And tomorrow morning, the same thing starts over again.
This explains why, today, several socialist countries must return to some sort of co-operation or participation, failing which they discourage freedom, security and initiative in the individual and prevent personal fulfillment.
Mr. Speaker, if the government genuinely serves the Canadian people, if it wishes the development of this country, if it wants all its citizens, young or not so young, to invest in Canada and share in its economic activity, it must give up such poultices and stop throwing dust in people's eyes. Mr. Speaker, it must take more direct, efficient and humane means and give each citizen, especially to the small wage earner, an opportunity to contribute to the economic activity of this country.
This is the heart of the matter, this is where the tragedy occurs. Those who rely for a living on welfare or veterans allowances, or on pensions, those who eke out a living, are directly dependent on society.
Our country is tremendously rich: it is an affluent nation. However, its poor are left to decay in poverty, to keep crawling. The leader of the Ralliement creditiste (Mr. Caouette) says very vividly and truthfully: Hardship exists among plenty. Though paradoxical, the remark is true.
The government, allegedly to help the humble people, the unemployed, the poor and the people on welfare, refuses to listen to their representations. Instead of really trying to solve their problems, by giving them the necessary funds to share in the economic activity of this country and also invest some money, it turns its head away and keeps providing incentives for the better off.
Not so long ago, I read an article which appeared in he Devoir and bore the signature of Mr. Brody, a lecturer at the Industrial Relations Department of the University of Montreal.
This reporter said that an economic policy is mostly a choice between several options.
The successive governments for many years never felt free to introduce such legislation because they were under the control of high finance.
I see that the Minister of Finance is frowning. That is all he can do before high finance, because he dares not speak. Here again is a proof of it: a bill is introduced about the CDC, a corporation at the service of high finance and not of the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, governing a country means first, to make a choice, and when you cannot make that choice, then you should pull aside. We are anxious to push these people aside, Mr. Spaker, because they seem unable to make that choice.
We have to choose between taking from the rich and giving a little to the poor or putting the economic system

March 2, 1971
Canada Development Corporation in the service of all Canadians, whatever their language, their race, their religion, the thickness of their wallets, their goodwill or their good heart. There will come a moment when this choice will have to be made.
There is a third choice: to put everybody on an equal footing and say: Today, we run the steam-roller; we crush all Canadians and have them all fit in the same mold.
Those are the three options.
Encourage the present system, get bogged down even further, change nothing, or else introduce rash reforms through white papers and millions of dollars, without ever attempting the monetary reform. That is the first option, and precisely the one the Minister of Finance opted for.
That is the choice made by the Progressive Conservatives and that is why we say that there is no difference between the two major parties.
There is a second option, that of socializing everyone, and a third, which we support aggressively, that of giving every Canadian, while respecting his freedom and his security, the necessary monetary power, on the basis of our Canadian production, so that he might receive the dividend based on our production.
Indeed, what is the objective of the Minister of Finance? That amounts to giving to a small group of persons, to big finance, the possibility of drawing dividends from the investments of the CDC.
Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance says that it is good, we say that it must be good for all Canadians. If that is good for a small group of persons in Canada, he must organize a similar system, not through the CDC but through the Bank of Canada, in order to give each Canadian enough purchasing power to buy our production and allow him too to get the benefit of his work, of his investment, of Canadian production.
Such is the spirit of Social Credit, Mr. Speaker. It is not a revolutionary spirit, but a spirit of reform aimed at putting money at the disposal of the human being so that the individual will be in a position where he will be able to use the money, not only to his personal advantage but also to that of all Canadians.
Evidently, neither the unemployed, nor the recipients of welfare, nor the physically handicapped are interested. And even if they were, they do not have the means required for participation in the economic life of the country.
If the government truly wants to give those people a chance to be real Canadians, if it has faith in the future of Canada, in Canada's resources, in the human value of the Canadian people, then what is it waiting for to give the Canadian people the monetary means permitting each citizen to receive his share in Canadian investments and Canadian production?
In short, Mr. Speaker, I am strongly against the bill because it will not solve the problem, because it diverts our attention from the real issue. Besides not being real solution-and this is worse-it moves us away from the

answer because it continues to patronize the financiers who already exploit Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, this bill not only does not solve anything, but it will further discourage Canadians from participating in economic activities. The gap between rich and poor will widen.
Mr. Speaker, this is a basic question. We in Canada are living in a climate of crisis and tension. Each Canadian is searching for his identity, whatever his language, his religion and his birth place. Everyone would like to do something for his country, because everyone from coast to coast has a feeling that there is something the matter.
Mr. Speaker, now is the time to bring in the only reform that this government, like those which preceded it, never dared introduce, namely a monetary reform whereby the Bank of Canada would be put at the service of the people of Canada. This would make it possible to distribute the difference between Canadian production and consumption as dividends so that every Canadian would receive his share of profit and production.
Mr. Speaker, those were the remarks I wanted to make. I hope the government will consider this proposal seriously and will agree to respect Parliament by listening to whatever the members of the opposition have to say. We are not here as members of the opposition wereby to object to legislation but mainly to submit proposals and express useful criticism. This is why I say that this bill not only will not solve the problem but that it will draw us further away from any true solution which would consist in putting money at the disposal of each and every Canadian through the Bank of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what brings me here this evening is the negotiation that is currently going on between Treasury Board and
I,	750 east coast ship repair workers at the Halifax dockyard and about 1,200 west coast ship repair workers at the Esquimalt dockyard. As anybody who was in the House earlier today is well aware, the groups on both coasts have taken strike votes after turning down a conciliation offer, or the latest offer from the employer, the government of Canada. In both cases the vote is in favour of a strike, so that very large ramifications arise from the fact that the government is not able to make peace with its dockyard employees.
I shall not deal with the whole of this problem, Mr. Speaker, because I am rather close to the scene in the Halifax area and since 1957 I have been working on the side of the east coast employees and trying to better their lot. I am rather hesitant, as well, because as a Maritimer and the member for Halifax-East Hants I have been annoyed at the discrepancy in the salaries for essentially the same type of work on the east and west coasts. There are other things that annoy me. One is that the bargaining group for these craftsmen was certified on January
II,	1968, and-believe it or not-it is now working on the agreement to be effective from October 1, 1968, to September 30, 1970. This makes the subject under discussion rather historical. However, the men involved have not been paid a proper wage for that period of time and now we have to start with the period since September 30, 1970, and bring their wages up to date. Some hon. members may recall the remarks of my colleague from Dart-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) who mentioned another group not involved in this dispute, unless the situation should change with the setting up of picket lines. I refer to the general workers in the dockyard, who also will be looking for an increase in salary.
Mr. Speaker, I think the shame of the matter is that when we set up bargaining legislation a couple of years ago we thought that steps would be taken to come to grips with bargaining positions and collective agreements within the public service of Canada. That has not been the case, despite the assurances given in committee. I was a member of that committee and believed those assurances. The fact is, however, that government bargaining with employees in those categories is hopelessly out of date.
What are we faced with now? A conciliation report was issued by Mr. R. Gallagher, chairman, Mr. Peter Sadlier-Brown, the union nominee, and Mr. James P. Nichol, the government nominee. Mr. Gallagher and Mr. Sadlier-Brown recommended, for the east coast, 37 cents more an hour this time around and 37 cents more an hour next time around, for a total increase of 74 cents. For the west coast they recommended 42 cents and 42 cents. This would have brought the east coast rate from $3.31 to $4.05 an hour and the west coast rate from $4.16 to $5. Mr. Nichol, the government nominee, proposed 27 cents and 29 cents for the east coast and 34 cents and 36 cents for the west coast. In its offer to the employees the government proposed a 42 and 42 cents formula for the west coast and a 28 and 28 cents formula for the east coast. In effect, this was taking the majority figure in the conciliation report for the west coast employees and the minority figure for the east coast employees.
This was so incredible that I immediately asked for leave under Standing Order 43 to have the matter debated in this House, but I was denied that opportunity. I suppose the enormity of the crime had not sunk in with hon. members because I asked for leave before anybody had learned what was going on. On subsequent days I asked questions. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has also asked questions as have my colleagues from Dartmouth-Halifax East and Moose Jaw.
I say that this is an outrage and everyone ought to ask questions about the government's approach in dealing with these employees. The odd thing is that under the new collective bargaining agreement many side issues were resolved very nicely. When the whole business is done with and this matter is part of the collective bargaining agreement, some of the long outstanding grievances will have been cleared up. Unfortunately, however, when you get down to the bread and butter issues you get down to wages.
