REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INCENTIVE GRANT TO MICRO-MAX PRODUCTS TO ESTABLISH PLANT IN MAGOG, QUEBEC-ASSISTANCE TO CANADIAN DRUG INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked a question of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) with respect to the $3.8 million incentive grant that had been made to Micro-Max Products Limited of Kalamazoo,
Michigan, to assist in establishing a drug plant in Magog, Quebec. The minister replied that the grant had been made according to the regulations of his department. When I attempted to follow up the question and inquire if grants had been made to hard pressed individual Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers, no reply was forthcoming.
I have raised this question in the adjournment debate because there seems to be a fundamental conflict in the government's attempts to assist in the development of truly Canadian industry. I would like to know from tonight's spokesman for the government why it is blowing hot and cold on this issue, in one instance saying we must support our native industry and on the other hand providing large incentive grants to companies which are obviously foreign-owned.
The independent Canadian pharmaceutical industry is relatively small. However, it has been playing a significant role in the continuing campaign to bring down the high cost of drugs in Canada. More recently, the independent segment has been hard pressed, largely because of the passing of Bill C-102 two years ago. That bill was piloted by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford). Instead of bringing down the high cost of drugs, even with the 12 per cent relief from federal sales tax, it has tended to threaten the one segment of the industry that had been making a substantial contribution in the war against pollution.
I do not have time to go into the subject in detail but there is an excellent article in the February issue of Executive magazine headed, "High-priced drugs are still, well, high-priced". The subheading reads, "And who really expected anything different?" Before the government moved to make compulsory licences mandatory on request, these small independents were carrying out the same kind of operation. Since Bill C-102 passed in 1969, 60 compulsory licences have been granted. All of these have been for importation, none for manufacturing. This has caused several unfortunate side effects with respect to the Canadian industry. It is downgrading the research activities of the larger companies. For example, Ayerst moved their research activity across the border into New York state because of the bill.
I would like to receive answers to the following specific questions. What steps have been taken by the government to financially strengthen the independent Canadian segment of the pharmaceutical industry as promised at the time Bill C-102 was passed? If possible, I would like the reply to be in terms of a figure for the grants that have been made to companies like Micro Chemicals, Empire Laboratories and Delmar Chemicals. If it is not possible to provide the information during the course of this discussion, perhaps it could be supplied in the form of a statement on motions or in a letter to myself.
We are all concerned about the continuing high cost of drugs in Canada. The Ontario government, through its Parcost program-that is, prescriptions at reasonable cost-has made the first real break in bringing down the

March 2, 1971

high cost of drugs. Another device talked about at the moment is bulk buying for hospitals, which would perhaps provide cheaper drugs through this particular outlet. I think it is quite unfair to penalize the small segment of the independent Canadian pharmaceutical industry, which pioneered in this field, by providing incentives assistance to American-based companies and on the other hand allowing existing Canadian independents to be absorbed by the larger American companies which are continually knocking at their door. I trust the government will take action to remove this anomaly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 11 I questioned the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) in regard to consequences arising out of an order in council issued by the government of British Columbia on October 22, 1970. This order in council declared it as public policy that no person teaching or instructing the youth of British Columbia in educational institutions receiving government support shall continue in the employment of the institution if they advocate the policies of the Front de Liberation du Quebec or the overthrow of democratically-elected government by violent means.
Five teachers from such institutions promptly challenged the authority of the British Columbia government to issue such an order in council. In the first place, they declared there is no law passed by the legislative assembly of British Columbia delegating to the executive council or the Lieutenant-Governor in Council the power to pass such an order in council. Secondly, they declared that such an order in council is ultra vires the powers of the province, falling within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada under the British North America Act. The case was slated to come up for trial before the Supreme Court of British Columbia on February 25.
Because of the fundamental issues involved, I asked the Minister of Justice two questions. First, does the federal government plan to intervene in support of the action brought by the five teachers against the government of British Columbia? Second, will the federal government challenge the constitutionality of the order in council? To the first question the minister's answer was in substance no. To the second his answer was silence. Neither answer indicated that he is prepared, as Minister of Justice to uphold the law of this country and the civil rights of the citizen which are endangered when it is flouted.
In defence of his government's action, the Attorney General of British Columbia declared that if the said order in council were passed without legislative authority-which he specifically denies-then it is merely a declaration of government policy, without binding effect, and that therefore the teachers have no reason for their action. Further, the Attorney General disputes the right of the plaintiffs to bring his action in the courts, alleging that none of them has a legal interest which allows the bringing of the suit. But there are features about this order in council which constitute an extremely dangerous threat to the civil liberties of teachers in British Columbia and which should call forth the active interest and involvement of the Minister of Justice, who is charged with protecting the fundamental rights of Canadian citizenship, including freedom of speech and expression.
The British Columbia order in council requires the dismissal of teachers in certain circumstances, but pro-

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion vides no guarantee that those accused and dismissed will be dealt with in accordance with what is usually called due process. There is no mention ol who is to judge whether persons accused are in fact guilty, whether they will have the right to know and face their accusers, the right to legal counsel, the right to cross-examine witnesses, the right to the other various safeguards which are essential. Apart from this backdoor attack on civil liberties, it should surely be the concern of the Minister of Justice to protect the federal jurisdiction. When a provincial government attempts to usurp powers which rightly belong to the federal government, it is extremely important that the federal Minister of Justice join in laying before the courts the reasons for striking down such attacks on federal powers.
History teaches that where civil liberties have been destroyed such destruction rarely, if ever, took place overnight; rather, there was an insidious, creeping erosion of the rights of the citizens to which those in authority turned the deaf ear and the blind eye. I appeal to the Minister of Justice to exercise his rightful authority in this case and to show the people of Canada that he is prepared to accept his full responsibility for protecting federal law and federal jurisdiction.

Consequently, as the Minister of Justice so aptly said in reply to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, the federal government and Department of Justice do not intend to intervene, and they never do, in an area of provincial jurisdiction.

Wednesday, March 3, 1971
